eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 10300/83) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 7 February 1983. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality. The Government, the Commission and the applicant appeared before the Court in Strasbourg in 1987. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by. Mr. Weitzel for the Commission, by Mr. Bergemann for the applicant, as well as their replies to its. questions. The applicant’s memorial - drafted in German - was lodged with the registry on 1 July 1986 and the Government's on 19 November. On 29 November, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court (Rule 50). Martha Nölkenbockhoff is the widow and heir of Mr. Theodor Nöelkenborkhoff. Her husband was a senior manager in a holding company, Stumm AG, whose trading activities centred on iron, steel and fuel. He was found guilty inter alia on several charges of breach of trust (Untreue), criminal bankruptcy (Bankrott) and fraud (Betrug) and given an aggregate sentence of eight years’ imprisonment. His four co-defendants were also sentenced to prison terms - two of them, for more or less identical offences and a few additional ones, to nine years, nine months. Mr. Nölkenbockhoff entered an appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November. Three of the co-defendants, who had likewise challenged the Regional Court’s judgment, later withdrew their appeals. The appeal lodged by the fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on 7 July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. The applicant sought orders that the Treasury should bear the necessary costs and expenses incurred by her late husband in connection with his conviction. The Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff on 5 March 1982. The defendant had already been found guilty, in a judgment that had not become final, after lengthy court proceedings in a trial (Hauptverhandlung) lasting more than three and a half years. The judgment convicting the three co-defendants ..., who were likewise sentenced to several years’ imprisonment, has become final. Three of the defendants ... have withdrawn their appeals on points of law, thereby confirming the judgment against them, argues decisively in favour of the correctness (materielle Richtigkeit) of the judgment. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand, pursuant to section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. In written pleadings dated 18 March, she challenged, inter alia, the Regional Court's finding that, had her husband not died, he “would almost certainly have been convicted”. She claimed that that statement was erroneous and infringed the Basic Law. The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant had requested an adjournment to await the judgment of the Federal Court of Justice in the appeal proceedings brought by one of the co-defendants. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceased. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss) of criminal proceedings, a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act (see paragraphs 24-26 below). And it added: “Even assuming such decisions are possible (Zulässigkeit), the assessment of the probable outcome of the trial, which must be made in both instances, leads to the conclusion that if the proceedings had been pursued until a final decision was handed down, the former defendant's conviction would almost certainly have been upheld” Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) claiming a breach of the Basic Law. A bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint because it considered that the complaint did not have sufficient prospects of success. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted. That does not mean, however, that in every case costs must be reimbursed where the proceedings are terminated without guilt having been established’ The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. Nor do the grounds advanced in support of the constitutional complaint show the unreasonableness of the Regional Court’s opinion that, had the proceedings been continued, a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal. The decision does not offend the presumption of innocence. Nor was the prediction of the outcome of the proceedings arbitrary in nature.

The applicant was expelled from the naval academy for failing his class twice. Claiming that his exam in Mathematics 1 had not been graded correctly, he demanded the reassessment of his paper in the relevant subject. The court acknowledged that the paper had indeed been misgraded, yet even the modified grade did not entitle the applicant to pass his class. The applicant subsequently retook the exams he had previously failed, yet failed them once again, which led to the issue of a second expulsion order by the naval academies. The written opinion submitted by the principal public prosecutor to the Supreme Military Administrative Court prior to the hearing was not communicated to the applicant.

On 11 December 1986, on an appeal by E., joined (Eintritt in den Rechtsstreit) by the agency, the Dülndorf Court of Appeal refused to grant an injunction prohibiting the applicant from systematically criticising the dDP. The judgment was based on section 1 of the 1909 Act, which provides: “Any person who, in the course of business commits, for purposes of competition, acts contrary to accepted moral standards may be enjoined from further engaging in those acts and held liable for damages’ The court held that in his circular the respondent had repeated in his own name the allegations made in the attached articles. Admittedly, he had sought to correct assertions made about him in the press release that were possibly false but he had acted above all for purposes. of competition. The distribution of the circular referring to the enclosed adverse newspaper reports on, inter alia, the [ddp]’s activities as a news agency was apt to enhance the competitive position of the respondent’S company. The respondent had already been planning for a long time to set up his own agency in the event of his leaving the [ddp]’s service. The circular and newspaper cuttings were sent out about a month later to selected addressees. It shows that the respondent intended to provoke discussion not only with a view to correcting assertions concerning himself that were possibly false. The last paragraph of the circular likewise makes the competitive intention clear. This is because even true statements may only be used to disparage a competitor where the person making them has sufficient reason to link his own competitive position with disparagement of the competitor and provided the criticism does not in nature or degree exceed what is necessary. The court noted that the prohibition in issue related solely to the applicant’s chosen method of circulating his information. The information was, moreover, of a business nature, but this did not mean that it ceased to be an opinion whose expression was protected by Article 5 para. 1, first sentence, of the Basic Law. This provision therefore had to be weighed against section 1 of the 1909 Act, on which the prohibition had been founded. The court went on: “In order for it to be determined how [freedom of expression and fair competition] are to be related to each other in the case of damaging comment by a competitor’” Freedom of expression takes precedence over rights (Rechtsgüter) protected by ordinary laws. The distribution of the applicant’s circular can hardly be regarded as an attempt to influence public opinion. It was designed almost exclusively to promote his private business interests and to secure or improve his competitive position in the news market. The fact that the impugned circular followed a press release directed against him which had been issued by the dDP did not invalidate this conclusion. In order to claim the protection of the Constitution, his response would have had to be intended to influencepublic opinion, which it was not. It follows that the finding by the Court of Appeal that the applicant's distribution of a circular was contrary to accepted moral standards is not incompatible with Article 5 para. 1 of the Basic Law. The Commission declared the application (no. 15088/89) admissible on 3 December 1991. In its report of 7 January 1993 (made under Article 31) (art. 31), it expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a violation of Article 10. (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (“the 1978 Act’; see paragraph 16 below) They were informed that they were being arrested under this section and that this was because the arresting officer suspected them of being terrorists. They were also told that they could be detained for up to 72 hours. No charges were brought against either applicant. The first applicant was released at 11.40 a.m. on 7 February 1986 and the second applicant five minutes later. Excluding the time taken to bring them to the police station, the first applicant had thus been detained 44 hours. The second applicant 44 hours and 5 minutes. He was informed at the time of his arrest that he was being arrested as he was suspected of being a terrorist. Mr Hartley was suspected of involvement in a kidnapping incident in Ballymena. Those involved in the kidnapping were thought to have connections with the Provisional IRA. The motive behind the kidnapping was believed to have been an attempt to force the young woman to retract an allegation of rape made the previous year as a result of which a person had been convicted and sentenced to 3 years’ imprisonment. He was released on 19 August 1986 at 2.10 p.m. after 30 hours and 15 minutes in detention. No charges were brought against him. He brought no proceedings in connection with his arrest or detention. In 1981, the nine last-mentioned applicants mounted an exhibition of contemporary art in Fribourg at the former Grand Seminary, a building due to be demolished. The ruling was upheld by the Supreme Court on 13 February 2009 and the case was dismissed.

The application claimed that the monitoring of his correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life under Article 8 of the convention. The case was decided to be heard by the Court of Appeal on 7 February 2008, and the judge ruled that the application should be allowed to stand.

The case originated in an application (no. 36936/05) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The application was made under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The application alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal, who ruled in favour of the applicant. The judge ruled that the application should be allowed to proceed. The decision was made on 7 February 2008, and the application was heard again on 11 February 2008.

The applicant suffered a brain haemorrhage in April 2001. He was sentenced to 14 years in prison in November 2001 for conspiracy to supply Class A drugs and two offences of possession of a Class A drug with intent to supply. The applicant wished to correspond confidentially with his external medical specialist to ensure that he would receive the necessary medical treatment and supervision in prison. He applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. In September 2002 the governor of the prison in which the applicant was being detained agreed to the applicant’s request. All outgoing and incoming mail was to be marked “medical in confidence”. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters.

The applicant was sentenced to 14 years in prison for conspiracy to supply Class A drugs and two offences of possession of a Class A drug with intent to supply. While on bail pending trial, the applicant suffered a brain haemorrhage for which he underwent surgery. Following his discharge to prison, he required monitoring and was required to go to hospital every six months for a specialist check-up by a neuro-radiologist. He expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence with his external medical specialist being read and applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. It was decided that the applicant’s medical correspondence would not be read.

C.I.A. applied for leave to appeal decision not to allow correspondence between him and his doctor. The judge ruled that the correspondence could continue, and that it was not illegal for the doctor to contact his patient in this way. The case was decided in favour of the doctor, and the case was dismissed by the Court of Appeal. The matter was adjourned until the end of next year, when the judge will make a new decision.

The Prison Service wanted to keep the prisoner's medical correspondence confidential. The court ruled that this was not a reason to allow the prisoner to keep his medical correspondence secret. The prisoner was allowed to continue to receive medical treatment from a doctor outside the prison. The case was heard at the Court of Appeal on February 18, 2004. The judge ruled that the prisoner was entitled to continue receiving treatment outside of the prison as long as he did not reveal the identity of the doctor or the location of the patient. eval_texts: The Buchholz case was referred to the Court by the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany. The case originated in an application against that State lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights on 18 December 1976. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. H. Mosler, the elected judge of German nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43) and Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court (Rule 21 par. 3) (b) of the Rules of Court. The President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members, namely Mr. Thór Vilhjálmsson and Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert. The Government’s memorial was received at the registry on 5 December. On 15 December, the Secretary to the Commission advised the Registrar that the Delegate would present his observations at the hearings. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 January. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government and by Mr. Gaukur Jörundsson and Mr. Sojka for the Commission, as well as their replies to questions put by the Court. At the hearings, the Agent of the Government made several documents available to the Court, and on 6 February the applicant and his lawyer supplemented in writing their answers to certain questions put to them. Mr. Buchholz was born in 1918 and lives in Hamburg. From February 1949 onwards he worked for the dry-cleaning firm of J. H. Dependorf KG. He was mainly employed as a driver until the end of 1963 and thereafter as, in particular, controller of branch establishments. On 28 June 1974, he was given notice that he was dismissed with effect from 31 December of the same year as a result of rationalisation measures. He took proceedings before the appropriate courts contesting the lawfulness of this notice; in his submission, those courts did not determine his case within “a reasonable time’. The Hamburg Labour Court of Appeal held that neither the notice of 28 June 1974 nor the extraordinary notice of 30 September 1974 had terminated the applicant’s contract. It ordered the defendants to pay Mr. Buchholz DM 5,700 arrears of wages but dismissed the claim for future salary. The Court also rejected an alternative request by the defendants for discharge (Auflösungsantrag) of the contract of employment in pursuance of section 7 of the Unfair Dismissal Act. The judgment was notified in writing to the parties on 25 February 1975 and the parties received it on 8 January 1975. Court of Appeal on 13 March 1975. Mr. Buchholz lodged a cross-appeal (Anschlussberufung) on 25 March, seeking payment of arrears of wages for the first three months of 1975. The parties then filed written pleadings dated 2 April and 15 May 1975 (the defendants) and 22 April (Mr. Buch Holz) The applicant maintained his accusations against the managers of the firm and asked the Court of Appeal to call for an expert’s opinion in order to corroborate the allegations made. The Court on 16 May 1975 set the case down for hearing on 22 July. On 20 August 1975, the defendants filed the chart, with accompanying explanations, on 31 July; then, on 6 August, they replied to a written pleading from Mr. Holz. The applicant put forward a proposal for a friendly settlement, but this was rejected by the defendants on 19 September. Mr. Buchholz’s lawyer filed a memorandum, dated 28 September, containing comments by his client and asked the Court to set the case down for an early hearing. On 9 October, the Court of Appeal decided to hold a hearing on 19 March 1976 and transmitted to the defendants the above mentioned written pleadings of 3 October. The legal and factual questions to be decided were debated by the two parties at the hearing held in March 1976. The Court proposed a settlement whereby the contract of employment would be considered as having terminated on 31 December 1974 and the defendants would pay the applicant a lump sum of DM 34,200. Mr. Buchholz denied that he had actually received the two notices of 30 September on that day. He asked the Court to question on his wife on this point, which was material for the purposes of Article 626 of the Civil Code. The applicant objected to such a move on the ground that it would tend to protract the proceedings. The Court nevertheless decided that Mr. Buch holz, as well as the chief executive of the Dependorf firm and the four witnesses nominated by the defendants, should be heard on 11 January 1977. At the same time it invited the applicant, who had applied for free legal aid in the appeal proceedings, to supply the necessary certificate. The case-file was sent to the Federal Constitutional Court which, sitting as a panel of three judges, gave judgment on 2 November. The Court refused leave for the constitutional application to proceed: even supposing the application to be admissible, it did not offer sufficient prospects of success. The Hamburg Chamber of Commerce, declared that the two disputed dismissal notices had indeed been received by Mr. Buchholz on 30 September 1974. On 13 May, the Court of Appeal ordered that an expert opinion should be obtained on the question whether or not the applicant’s accusations against the managers of the Dependorf firm were justified (see paragraph 15 above). Mr. Buchholz applied on 13 April to the Federal Labour Court for free legal aid. on being so requested, nominated an expert on 14 June. After hearing the parties, the Court appointed the expert on 30 June. The expert’s report was filed on 2 December 1977; the Court communicated it to the applicant and the defendants for comment by 5 January 1978. The last hearing was held on 3 February. The parties made their final submissions, following which the Labour Court of Appeal delivered its judgment. It allowed the defendants’ appeal and dismissed the applicant's cross-appeal, awarding the costs of the proceedings against him. On 26 April 1979, the Federal Court proposed a settlement whereby the contract of employment would be considered as having terminated on 31 December 1974. The applicant took his case to the Federal Constitutional Court alleging violation of several basic rights. He complained of the length of the proceedings before the various labour courts, citing this factor as the cause of the contested decision. On 19 July, the Constitutional Court refused leave for the constitutional application to proceed on the ground that it was inadmissible. As in 1976 (see paragraph 28 above), the Court had sat in judgment as a panel of three judges. The applicant has been in receipt of a social security retirement pension (Sozialversicherungsrente), the amount of which – originally DM 1,462 per month - has been periodically adjusted. The labour courts of appeal experienced a significant increase in their workload between 1974 and 1976. The incidence of appeals from labour court judgments rose, as compared with the previous year, by 23.1 per cent in 1974. The average length of proceedings progressed from 2.88 months in 1974 to 3.20 months in 1975, but then fell to 2.98 months in 1976, 2.79 months in 1977 and 2.53 months in 1978. The Government tabled in the legislative assemblies in 1978 a Bill designed, amongst other things, to expedite proceedings before the labour courts. The resultant Act entered into force on 1 July 1979. On 7 December 1977, the Commission declared the application admissible. The Commission expressed the opinion that the requirements of Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) had not been observed. The Government made the following final submission, which had been indicated in their memorial of 5 December 1980: “[We] request a finding that the Convention has not been violated in the instant case.’’ The Court of Appeal ruled that no issue arose under Articles 3, 8 or 12. The decision was upheld by the European Court of Human Rights on 24 January 1981. The case is still pending at the Court of Appeals.

The application was brought by a group of five people who claimed that they had been denied equal protection under the European Convention on Human Rights. The ECHR ruled that they were entitled to apply for protection under Article 4 of the EU Human Rights Act of 1998, which provides for the right to sue for damages in the event of discrimination.

The application was brought by a group of people claiming to have been victims of abuse by their former employer. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Chamber decided to dismiss the application on 1 April 2003. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the Government had failed to exhaust its domestic remedies. The case was referred to the European Court of Justice (ECJ) on 15 January 2003. It was heard by a panel of three judges who decided in favour of the applicants. The decision was made by the ECJ on 11 January 2003 and the decision was published on 17 January. The ECJ ruled that the application was not admissible as it had not been brought by the applicant association and that the case was dismissed.

The total number of landowners affected by the dam's construction is 159. By a ministerial decree of 2 November 1990, the Ministry of Public Works adopted the project. In 1991 the villages and the applicant association brought an administrative appeal before the Audiencia Nacional against the ministerial decree. The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the procedure for informing the public about the proposed dam. Finally, the court's attention was drawn to the project's impact on the nature reserves within the relevant area.

Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) would be the Court's Fourth Section. The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. According to the Government, the total number of landowners affected by the dam's construction is 159. On 1 April 2003 the Chamber decided, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to dismiss a Rule 39 request submitted by the applicants. The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the project. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal on 15 April 2003. The decision was unanimous. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal, considering in particular that, according to the law, the planned dam should have been based on the national hydrological plan. The court also accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam. On 17 June 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Autonomous. Community Law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. This law amended Aut autonomous Community Law no. 6/1987 of 10 April 1987, particularly with regard to the possibility of reclassifying the protection zone or carrying out. In the meantime, Counsel for the State and the government of the Autonomous Community of Navarre had appealed on points of law against the Audiencia Nacional's judgment of 29 September 1995. In a judgment of 14 July 1997, the Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves RN 9, 10 and 11. As a result of the judgment, the size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz, where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. In the alternative, the applicant association requested that certain provisions in the Aut autonomous Community law be referred to the Constitutional Court for a preliminary ruling on their constitutionality. The Constitutional Court declared the issues raised in the preliminary question admissible by a decision of 21 July 1998. The government and parliament of Navarre submitted their observations on 11 and 15 September 1998 respectively. Under section 37(2) of the Judicature Act, it gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the government and Parliament and invited them to file their observations within fifteen days. The Audiencia Nacional forwarded to the Constitutional Court the written pleadings submitted by the applicant association during the proceedings before it. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 had become impossible since the entry into force of the new law. The court also ruled that, given the significance of the question raised by the Itoiz dam's construction, which could not simply be ignored, it was justifiable that the explanatory memorandum accompanying the law specifically mentioned the aim and means of environmental protection in the peripheral protection zones.  Constitutional Court considered that in the meantime a new law had been passed amending the legal system applicable to the peripheral protection zones. It found that both the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 and the new Autonomous Community law of 1996 were intended to guarantee the existence of a peripheral protection zone around the three nature reserves affected by the dam's construction. The balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. Consequently, the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 § 1 of the Constitution. It added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation, being general in form and in substance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. It was. out that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy. provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. The application was dismissed by the court and no further action was taken by the Government. The case was decided in favour of the government by the Court of Appeal and the judgment was announced in April 2000, and the case was dismissed on 15 April 2000 by the Supreme Court of Justice and the High Court of the Republic of South Africa. The ruling was published as part of a series of articles in the official Gazette at the time.

The interrogation was transmitted via a sound link and the witness’ voice was distorted in order to protect the witness' anonymity. The applicant and his counsel were allowed to put additional questions to X. The latter refused to answer a number of questions which the defence counsel considered to be important, notably the following: “Why had X arranged a meeting with N.b.? How did X react after the crime?"

The court considered that the testimony given by X was credible and pertinent. It noted that X had submitted in a credible and convincing way that his life was in danger in case he testified. The applicant had a motive to take revenge on the witness who had contributed to his conviction and to prevent him from making further testimonies. The court had taken a number of measures to compensate the restrictions imposed on the rights of the defence. It had thus been known that the witness had no criminal record and that there was no indication that he had any contact with the drug trafficking scene. There was further no indication of X having been in any way involved in the drug-trafficking.

The jury court convicted the applicant of manslaughter (vorsätzliche Tötung) and of several counts of drug-trafficking and sentenced him to fourteen years and nine months’ detention. The patient was transferred to a hospital in Ankara for treatment. He was discharged from the military in 2002. He sought compensation from the Ministry of the Interior for the damage he had suffered. The court ruled that he could not be compensated for the loss of his eye sight because there had been no doctor present when he needed treatment. The patient was awarded a total of 30,000,000 Turkish liras (EUR) for his eye damage. He also received a compensation package of 20,500,000 (Eur) for the time he spent in hospital. He has also received an apology from the Turkish government for the delay in his treatment. Three university professors from the ophthalmology department of Gazi University’s Faculty of Medicine were appointed as experts in the case. Their expert report drawn up on 6 April 2005 concluded: “Our medical opinion, based on our examination of the plaintiff's allegations, is as follows: ‘We are of the opinion that there were no delays, shortcomings, mistakes or negligence in the steps taken in transferring the patient to the hospital, diagnosing the problem, treating the problem or treating the patient’’ The applicant submitted a written statement to the administrative court on 29 April 2005, arguing that the medical report contained contradictory conclusions. He pointed out that, although the experts had indicated in the report that the problem had not been fully diagnosed, they had then gone on to conclude that there had been no shortcomings. On 18 May 2005 the Supreme Military Administrative Court, on the basis of the expert report of 6 April 2005, dismissed the applicant’s claim by a majority of four to one and held that no fault could be attributed to the military authorities in the treatment of the applicant. A dissenting judge stated in his separate opinion that issues such as the cause of the problem and what bearing the one-to-two week delay had had on the outcome had not been established. The applicant requested a rectification of the administrative court's decision, but it was refused. They noted that section 71(1) imposed a positive duty to proceed with confiscation proceedings. The prime purpose behind the statutory provision for confiscation orders was the recovery of any financial benefit that an offender might have obtained from his criminal conduct. Though no common law power to adjourn existed, Parliament could not have intended to disable a court from making a confiscation order after sentence merely because the time-limits were not strictly adhered. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40378/10) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a parent of two young children, is a homeless person in priority need of accommodation within the meaning of Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 (“the 1996 Act”) Birmingham City Council determined that the applicant was homeless, eligible for assistance and not intentionally homeless. The authority accepted that it owed the applicant the “main housing duty” to provide accommodation to her and her family. The applicant viewed the property on 19 March 2007 but declined the offer as she was not happy with the condition of the communal area. The Council said that, by reason of her rejection of its offer, pursuant to section 193 of the Housing Act its duty to her under Part VII of the 1996 Act had been discharged. By letter dated 29 March 2007 the applicant notified the Council that she had not received an offer in writing and requested that the Council review its decision. While the applicant’s case was pending before the review panel, a further offer of accommodation was made to her pursuant to a different scheme, namely the scheme for the provision of housing accommodation. She did not accept this offer. The appeal was heard on 29 August 2007, on which date the judge noted that the only ground of appeal argued before him was that the letter of offer had failed to arrive. The applicant submitted that the County Court should hear evidence on the matter so that it could determine it for itself. Although the judge accepted that the Homelessness Review Officer was not an independent or impartial tribunal, he found that the decision whether or not the letter had been received was properly and fairly to be made by her. Although it was not specifically stated in the correspondence between the Council and the applicant, the judge appeared to consider if the Council had discharged its duty under section 193(7) (see paragraph 25 below) House of Lords stressed that although the Officer had been called upon to resolve some disputed factual issues, these findings of fact were “only staging posts on the way to the much broader judgments” concerning local conditions and the availability of alternative accommodation. Officer could not be regarded as independent, since she was employed by the Council which had made the offer of accommodation which the claimant had rejected. But statutory regulations provided substantial safeguards to ensure that the review would be independently and fairly conducted. Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 7 November 2008. In doing so, it proceeded on the assumption that the case involved the determination of the applicant's civil rights for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Thomas LJ concluded that the decision of the House of Lords in Runa Begum applied to all County Court appeals under section 204 of the 1996 Act, no matter whether the decision turned on a simple issue of primary fact or not. The decision in Tsfayo, which concerned the housing benefit scheme, did not affect appeals brought in homelessness cases, he added. He concluded: “It is clear from the careful judgments of Judge MacDuff QC and Judge McKenna that both considered that the housing authority had fairly treated both appellants in cases where the determinative issue was a question of fact’” The ruling has ‘significant implications for not only the statutory scheme but for the court and tribunal system’ The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, finding that the determination by the Council, that its duty to secure accommodation for the applicant had ceased, was not a determination of her civil rights within the meaning of Article 6.1. Lord Hope of Craighead stated that: “... I would be prepared now to hold that cases where the award of services or benefits in kind is not an individual right of which the applicant can consider himself the holder, do not engage article 6(1). In my opinion they do not give rise to ‘civil rights’ within the autonomous meaning that is given to that expression for the purposes of that article” The court went on to observe that the fact that a County Court did not have a full fact-finding jurisdiction when hearing an appeal under section 204 of the 1996 Act did not mean that the applicant was deprived of what was required to satisfy the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention. Lord Hope said that the possibility, foreshadowed in argument, of separating simple, formal questions of “gateway” facts, such as the letter issue, from the expert assessment of suitability would needlessly complicate a scheme which was designed to be simple to administer. Unlike the County Court, the Supreme Court appeared to consider whether or not the Council had discharged its duty to the applicant under section 193(5); however, it appeared to accept that a formal letter of offer was required.

On March 21, 1991, the Secretary of State revoked his licence. This was because of reports that he had lied to his supervising officers and avoided telling them of significant events following his release. Mr Singh was also arrested and charged with fraud and using threatening behaviour. He denied the charges and was released in May 1991. In August 1991, he was sent a letter explaining why his licence had been revoked. This explains how he was able to return to the community he had lived in since his release from prison.

Mr Singh denied the accuracy of most of the allegations against him. He asked the Parole Board to review the merits of the revocation of his licence. Under section 62 (4) of the Criminal Justice Act 1967 the Board was empowered at this stage to take a binding decision for Mr Singh’s immediate release. On 19 December 1991 the Board decided against recommending Mr Singh's immediate release and he was not told the reasons for this decision. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend Mr Singh. The applicant then sought judicial review. On 20 April 1993 the Divisional Court quashed the Board's decision. Lord Justice Evans found that the applicant was entitled to a fresh consideration.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 8 December 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 23389/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 25 January 1994 by a British citizen, Mr Prem Singh. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 4 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the case of Hussain v the United UK should be heard by the same Chamber. Mr Prem Singh was convicted at Leeds Crown Court of the murder of a 72-year-old woman in 1973. Mr Singh received a mandatory sentence of detention “during Her Majesty’s pleasure’ pursuant to section 53 (1) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1933 (as amended) (see paragraph 29 below) In October 1990, having served the punitive part of his sentence (“tariff” - see paragraph 33 below), Mr Singh was released on licence. On 11 March 1991 the applicant was arrested and interviewed at Southmead. On 27 September 1995 the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. On 21 March 1991 his life licence was revoked by the Secretary of State on its recommendation. Mr Singh was charged with a number of alleged offences involving deception, and one of using threatening behaviour. He denied the allegations, and asked the Parole Board to review the merits of the revocation of his licence. On 19 December 1991 the Board decided against recommending Mr Singh’s immediate release. The case was heard at the Crown Prosecution Service and the Appeal Court. The Appeal Court ruled in favour of Mr Singh, and he was released on bail. The appeal was heard and the appeal was dismissed on 25 December 1991. The application was returned to the Probation Service, and Mr Singh returned to prison. Prem Singh was jailed in 1991 after being convicted of misconduct in a public office. The criminal charges against him were dismissed because the prosecution had presented the indictment out of time. Mr Singh asked for his case to be reconsidered in the light of this development, and the Secretary of State referred it back to the Parole Board. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend Mr Singh’s release. He was not told the reasons for this decision. The applicant then sought judicial review (see paragraph 47 below) of the two decisions. On 20 April 1993 the Divisional Court quashed the decision of 19 December 1991 on the ground that there had been a breach of natural justice. The court held that the applicant was entitled to a fresh consideration. Prem Singh was released from prison in 1994. He was offered a review of his case by the Parole Board. The Secretary of State refused to accept the Board's release recommendation. Mr Singh was not permitted to be present at the review and had no opportunity to give oral evidence or to question those who had made allegations against him. He applied for a judicial review of this decision, but he withdrew his application on or about 7 March 1994 because he had been offered an early review. The applicant was also informed on 21 July 1994 that the Secretary of state was “not prepared to accept this recommendation and [did not agree] to [the applicant’s] release“. Prem Singh was recalled to prison “following serious breaches of the trust placed in [him] as a life licensee’s decision’. He had misled the probation service after his release in October 1990 and had appeared before the magistrates on several criminal charges, although these had subsequently been dismissed on technical grounds. The Secretary of State was unable to assess accurately whether he was still a threat to the public, because he had spent the three and a quarter years since his recall in a closed prison. On 16 March 1995 the Divisional Court quashed the Secretary of. State's decision and ordered him to reconsider it. In September 1995 Mr Singh joined a pre-release employment scheme.

They were released from custody on licence on 22 May 2003 and 18 January 2002 respectively. They both travelled to Spain without notification, thereby breaching the terms of their parole licence in contravention of the Sex Offenders Act 1997. The Scottish Executive subsequently revoked their licences. They pled guilty and on 4 April 2005 they were sentenced to a further three years’ imprisonment, which was reduced on appeal to eighteen months. On 5 April 2005 a decision was made by the Procurator Fiscal to place both applicants on petition in relation to the murder of A.M. The applicants’ had subsequently killed her and disposed of her body. The applicants were charged with the murder of A.M. and with concealing and disposing of her body in an attempt to pervert the course of justice. On 6 June 2005 the Crown Office provisionally fixed a preliminary hearing date for 12 September 2005. That hearing date was set aside as the first applicant lodged a “devolution minute’ (see paragraphs 51-52 below) relating to a potential violation of the reasonable time guarantee. A Proof of Life report was produced on 18 November 2005 (supplemented on 5 January 2006), which concluded that A.m. had been dead since approximately June 1997. The twelve-month period for bringing proceedings expired on 4 April 2006. The applicants were charged in relation to the disappearance of A.M. Spain for a period before returning to the United Kingdom in November 2007. The police continued to conduct periodic reviews of the decision to take “no proceedings meantime’ in respect of the 2005 petition. Central Scotland Police formed “Operation Aspen’, the objective of which was to look for evidence both of further sexual offending by the applicants, and of their involvement in the disappearance. New evidence came to light as a result of Operation Aspen concerning the circumstances of the disappearance and the applicants’ sexual offending. On 9 September 2008 Crown Counsel concluded that there had been a material change in the prospects of securing a conviction against both applicants on the murder charges. The first applicant argued that the murder charge against him should be dismissed for reason of delay. However, the court refused to dismiss the charge, finding, inter alia, that proceedings had begun on 5 April 2005. The applicants’ trial for the sexual offences took place between 19 April 2010 and 13 May 2010. On 12 May 2010 the applicants were convicted on numerous counts and sentenced to periods of imprisonment ranging from eight to ten years to run concurrently. They were sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, with a tariff of thirty years for the first applicant and twenty-six years forThe second applicant. They unsuccessfully sought to appeal against conviction and sentence. First applicant lodged a Note of Appeal on 2 September 2010, containing numerous grounds and sub-grounds on a wide range of issues regarding all the charges. The sifting judges granted him leave to appeal against his sentence for murder, but not against his conviction. The applicants subsequently applied under section 107(8) of the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 (‘the 1995 Act’) for leave to reinstate grounds which the judges had found to be unarguable, including those relating to the length of proceedings. A hearing took place on 29 and 30 April 2013 before the Supreme Court, which gave judgment on 13 June 2013. The court assessed the evidence in light of the relevant case-law of the domestic courts and of this Court. Supreme Court observed that as the ‘fair trial’ guarantee under Article 6 was distinct from the “reasonable-time” guarantee it had to be approached separately. The court concluded that the correct “starting point” in the applicants’ proceedings was 5 April 2005 and the case was remitted to the Appeal Court. It is not a condition for the examination of civil compensation claims that the accused person should have been convicted in respect of the charge. The injured party, who does not enjoy rights as a party in the criminal case, should not forfeit his or her compensation claim as a result of an acquittal. Even assuming that the Convention provision applies to the treatment of such claims, it has not been infringed as long as no disagreement or doubt has been expressed with regard to the decision on criminal liability. It is above all the High Court’s decision concerning compensation which has been brought before the Supreme Court under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The injured party, who does not enjoy rights as a party in the criminal case, should not forfeit his or her compensation claim as a result of an acquittal. By Article 6 § 2 of the Convention, a person who is charged with a criminal offence is to be deemed innocent until proved guilty. However, in my opinion it must be clear that the said provision cannot constitute an obstacle for a person injured by an act to claim compensation from the alleged perpetrator, even though the latter has been acquitted. After hearing the parties and a large number of witnesses, the Supreme Court, in a judgment of 5 June 1996, ordered the applicant to pay NOK 75,000 to G. in compensation for non-pecuniary damage, under section 3-5(1)(1) Under Chapter 29 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, civil compensation claims may ... be made in criminal proceedings by the prosecution or by the injured party. By Article 6 § 2 of the Convention, a person who is charged with a criminal offence is to be deemed innocent until proved guilty. The presumption of innocence applies even after an acquittal. The court in such a case can rely on a finding that the defendant has in fact committed the act in relation to which he has been acquitted. Even assuming that the Convention provision applies to the treatment of such claims, it has not been infringed as long as no disagreement or doubt has been expressed with regard to such claims. The Supreme Court found that the evidence satisfied the standard of proof, establishing that sexual abuse had occurred and that, on the balance of probabilities, it was clear that the applicant was the abuser. There was a basis for awarding the victim compensation under section 3-5(1)(b) of the Damage Compensation Act. However, Justice Gjølstad emphasised that this decision was taken independently of the decision in the criminal case and that it did not undermine the acquittal. ‘I cannot see that the arrangement under Norwegian criminal procedural law, whereby it is possible to have civil compensation claims determined after an acquittal, gives rise to any particular problems in relation to Article 6 § 2 [of the Convention].’ G. found that several infringements had occurred and that, even though their extent was not possible to ascertain with precision, there had been serious violations involving a certain use of force or threats, as a result of which G. had sustained damage. G. was found to have committed several violations of the terms of his contract. G was also found to be guilty of two counts of misconduct in a public office, as well as one count of breach of a court order. The court also found that G had committed a breach of his contract with the United States of America, and that he had breached his contract with the U.S. government.

The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in Nicosia. He stated that he had been living in a house in Kyrenia and was the owner of a field with trees in the village of Ayios Epiktitos. He was being continuously prevented from entering the northern part of Cyprus because of his Greek-Cypriot origin. On 9 December 1990 the applicant made one further attempt to return to his property in northern Cyprus by participating in a convoy of cars of fellow refugees intending to return home during a peaceful march towards their villages. The applicant and his fellow refugees, who had informed the Commander of the United Nations (UN) forces in Cyprus of their intentions, stopped at the check point in the “buffer zone”. There, they asked the UN officer on duty to be allowed to returnto their homes, property and villages.

As a result of the 1974 Turkish military intervention he had been deprived of his property rights. His property was located in the area which was under the occupation and the overall control of the Turkish military authorities. The latter had prevented him from having access to and using his house and property. He was being continuously prevented from entering the northern part of Cyprus because of his Greek-Cypriot origin. He acquired ownership of this property on 27 June 1990, when it was transferred to him by way of inheritance from his grandfather and a gift from his parents.

Kamuran Alican, Çetin Alican and Ilhami Alican took their animals out to graze. The children were grazing their sheep in the field when they found an object with an iron head which looked like a bullet. The first applicant left the other two children to find water while they were trying to hit the iron head with pieces of metal. At that moment the bullet exploded. As a result of the explosion, the first applicant suffered partial loss of the sight of one eye and the total loss of sight in the other. The second and third applicants' sons were killed. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal of Turkey.

The applicants were born in 1983, 1946 and 1936 respectively. The application concerns the wounding of the first applicant, who was eleven years old at the time, and the death of the second and third applicants' sons, Çetin Alican and İlhami Alican, who were fourteen and thirteen years old respectively. It concerns the explosion of an RPG-7 (anti-tank grenade launcher) grenade outside the applicants' village, Kıyıdüzü, in Van. The first applicant suffered partial loss of the sight of one eye and the total loss of sight in the other as a result of the explosion.

The children had collected a grenade from an RPG-7 grenade launcher and parts of a rocket and were trying to explode them. They received no positive reply. The decision of the military prosecutor was served on 29 May 1997 on Ahmet Alican,. on 7 July 1997 on Kamuran  and on 19 July 1997  on Ramazan Alican.

The case of Ahmet Alican is one of the most famous in the history of the Turkish court system. The application for compensation for damage caused by an accident involving the Ministry of Defence was made in 1994. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment as regards the amount of compensation awarded but quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the latter had failed to determine which administrative entity had responsibility for compensating the applicant. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and this case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. By a decision of 30 November 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant’s late father had applied on 13 June 1989 to the Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) of Lund for tentative approval (förhandsbesked) of a plan to divide Humanisten 1 and build a new one-family house. The purpose of such an approval, issued under Chapter 8, section 34 of the 1987 Act, was to give a property owner who was planning a building project for which the grant of a building permit was uncertain the possibility to obtain an advance assessment of whether the planned measures may be permitted at all. According to the detailed development plan in force, only one main building was allowed on the existing property plot. On 15 April 1992 the Building Committee granted the applicant a tentative approval of a plan to divide the plot – Humanisten 1 – and to build a new one-family house. Several of the applicant’s neighbours opposed the measure with reference to the special character of the neighbourhood. At the beginning of March 1993 the Land Survey recommended that the property plan be repealed in order to facilitate a division of the property enabling the applicant to construct a new house on the resulting new plot. A new property plan would not be required; repeal of the existing property plan was sufficient. On 17 March 1993, the building committee followed the Land Surveys suggestion and repealed the plan. Owners of two neighbouring properties appealed against the decision to the Board, claiming that the neighbourhood was worthy of preservation due to its special character. The Board visited the area before deciding on 24 September 1993 to reject the appeal. The neighbours appealed to the Government, invoking the same grounds as before the Board. On 14 November 1996 the Government quashed the Board’s decision to repeal the property plan for Humanisten 1. The Government find that the suitability of the intended change of the property and the development conditions within the block ought to be examined through a new detailed development plan for the area in which the size and situation of the buildings can also be regulated to a sufficient extent. Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant’s request on the ground that the case could be examined and decided without holding an oral hearing. Court found that the Government's decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. A request by the applicant for re-opening of the case was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court on 10 April 2002. The applicants are jointly and severally liable for paying legal costs of DKK 62,250.” ‘There is only one approved chemotherapy against pleural mesothelioma cancer, but that is not offered to SP [one of the patients followed in the programme]. The doctors chose to treat her with a substance not approved for the diagnosis, and whose effect on Pleural meso-cerebral cancer is not substantiated’ Close to 300 patients in Denmark have been given test medication. In the worst scenario, that may result in patients dying earlier than if they had been given the approved medication. Two of the patients who were interviewed have passed away. The programme gives the impression that malpractice has occurred at Copenhagen University Hospital, in that S has deliberately used medication (Vinorelbine) which is not approved for treatment of pleural mesothelioma cancer, says the narrator. The money has been paid into S’s personal research account. DKK 90,000 is earmarked for the tests. S withheld that information. S will not acknowledge what leading experts agree on; that Alimta is the only medication whose effect is substantiated. The applicants, as producer of the programme and as chief sub-editor, have made an allegation against Copenhagen University Hospital and S of malpractice and of nourishing irrelevant considerations. The way that the programme is built up with its beginning and ending, the viewers get the clear impression that the reasons behind this choice of medication [Vinorelbine] were S’s professional prestige and personal finances. The applicants have not attempted to establish the truth of the allegation, but have submitted that the allegation shall be unpunishable by virtue of Article 269 (1) of the Penal Code as they acted in lawful protection of an obvious public interest or the interest of others. Copenhagen's High Court: The applicants made allegations based on an incorrect factual basis. The aim of the programme is to make a critical assessment of the treatment of patients with pleural mesothelioma cancer offered by Copenhagen University Hospital and the responsible consultant. But it cannot justify an allegation, which is built on a factually incorrect basis, and thus a wrong premise. It is an aggravating factor that the wrongful accusations were disseminated on national television during primetime and on DR’s homepage, by means of which the accusations had a significant spread. The allegations are not unpunishable under Article 269 (1), nor is there any basis for remitting the punishment under Article269 (2) Four complaints were lodged with the Patient Insurance Association (Patientforsikringen) relating to the issues raised by the DR programme. All four complaints have been refused, one of the reasons being that the independent medical oncologists who assessed the cases found that it was in compliance with optimum medical standards. Two of the cases have been appealed against to the National Agency for Patients’ Rights and Complaints (Patientskadeankenævnet) The other appeal does not concern the issue of combination therapy. The applicants shall be jointly and severally liable for paying legal costs of the High Court appeal to Copenhagen University Hospital and S, in the amount of DKK 90,000.

A man was taken to a police station for identification purposes in November 1997. He refused to participate in an identification parade. A video of his actions was recorded and shown to witnesses. The police did not inform the man or his solicitor of its use. The judge ruled that the video should be admitted as evidence. The case was heard again in February 1999 when the judge was unable to sit. The applicant was found not guilty of the charge of unlawful interception of evidence. He was sentenced to five years in prison and a fine of £1,000. The trial was adjourned until January 1999. The conviction was later quashed and the case was dismissed.

The video was used for identification purposes. The judge concluded that there had been no unfairness arising from the use of the video. Eleven persons had been filmed for comparison purposes rather than the required eight. The video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant as involved in the second and fourth robberies. In his ruling of 26 February 1999, he found that the police had failed to comply with paragraphs D.11, D.2.15 and D.16 of the Code of Practice, inter alia with regard to their failure to inform the applicant of its creation, to inform him of its use in an identification parade, and of his own rights in that respect.

The applicant was taken from Strangeways Prison to the Bilston Street police station. A compilation tape was prepared in which eleven volunteers imitated the actions of the applicant. This video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant as involved in the second and fourth robberies. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor were informed that a tape had been made or used for identification parade purposes or given an opportunity to view it prior to its use. In his ruling of 26 February 1999, he found that the police had failed to comply with paragraphs D.2.11, D.3.15 and D.4.16 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984.

The applicant complained that the police covertly videotaped him for identification purposes and used the material in the prosecution against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The Court declared the application partly admissible in a decision of 26 September 2002. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. No hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The applicant was born in 1964 and is currently detained in HM Prison Brixton. He is alleged to have committed a series of armed robberies of mini-cab drivers. The applicant was charged in three armed robberies in 1997. He did not appear for identification parades. Two witnesses positively identified him as one of the robbers. A compilation tape was prepared in which eleven volunteers imitated the actions of the applicant as captured on the covert video. This video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant. The applicant was acquitted on all counts of the robbery charges. He was also acquitted on the counts of two other counts of armed robbery, one of which he was charged with in August 1997, but later acquitted on this count as well. The case was heard at the Old Bailey in 1998. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor were informed that a tape had been made or used for identification parade purposes or given an opportunity to view it prior to its use. 11 persons had been filmed for comparison purposes rather than the required eight and were all within comparative height, age and appearance. Even though the applicant's solicitor was not present to verify the procedures adopted when the witnesses were shown the videos, the entire process had been recorded on video and this had been shown to the court. The judge ruled that the evidence was therefore admissible. The trial lasted 17 days, the applicant and 31 witnesses giving live evidence. In his summing-up to the jury, the trial judge warned the jury at considerable length about the ‘special need for caution’ before convicting any defendant in a case turning partly on identification evidence. Jury convicted applicant of three counts of robbery and acquitted him of two others. The judge sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. The applicant applied for leave to appeal against conviction, inter alia, alleging that the trial judge had erred in not excluding the evidence obtained as a result of the covert identification video. Leave was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal. On 14 April 2000, the House of Lords rejected the application. The solicitors claimed that they were informed on 7 July 2000 that the jury had been told that the video evidence was not a fair test. The jury was also made aware of the alleged breaches of the code of practice.

Peter Maxwell was convicted of assault in the High Court of Justiciary at Kilmarnock, Scotland. The jury found him guilty of the charge and he was sentenced to five years' imprisonment. After conviction he instructed a new firm of solicitors, who then asked counsel who had represented him at the trial to advise on the prospects of an appeal. The solicitors informed the applicant that they could not identify any basis for an appeal and accordingly could not act for him. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. Ryssdal, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Emberland, Attorney, Attorney General’s Office (Civil Affairs). The applicant complained that the reasons stated by the Borgarting High Court in refusing to admit his appeal had been inadequate and thus entailed breach of Article 6 § 1 of the convention. The applicant sued Ekheim Invest claiming that he had title to 50% of the Ekheim estate. The question was how to interpret the former spouses’ joint ownership agreement of 3 November 1995. The applicant claimed that in the period since 2001 the estate had increased so greatly in value that the City Court now had to assess the ownership issue independently of the conclusion reached in the 2001 judgment. The City Court agreed with the applicant and said that the case should be decided on the basis of the parties’ relationship rather than the judgment as a main rule. The case was returned to the Court of Appeal on 8 July 2007 for further proceedings to be heard. The applicant appealed against the City Court’s judgment of 21 January 2008 to the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett) In a unanimous decision (beslutning) of 12 June 2008 the High Court concluded that it refused to admit the appeal (“Anken nektes fremmet”), giving the following reasons: “The High Court finds it clear that the appeal will not succeed, and that its admission should therefore be refused pursuant to Article 29-13(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure” The applicant appealed the decision to the Supreme Court, but lost. The Appeals Leave Committee of the Supreme Court (Høyesteretts ankeutvalg) rejected the appeal under Article 30-9 (2) arguing notably that the refusal of admission of the appeal lacked reasons. The 2005 Code of Civil Procedure (Tvisteloven) entered into force on 1 January 2008. The conditions for the High Court granting leave to appeal and for refusing the admission of an appeal (“Krav til samtykke. Nektelse”) were set out in Article 29-13 (5) of the 2005 Code. The High Court could dismiss (avvise) an appeal on the ground that is suffered from errors that ought to lead to dismissal or discontinue the proceedings in whole or in part. The High Court’s refusal of admission of an appeal was that the judgment appealed against gained legal force. The Ministry of Justice observed that an unlimited and extensive right in this respect could be counterproductive to the rule of law. The aim of introducing a merits filtering mechanism before the High Court was to promote the interests of procedural economy. The type of decision (beslutning) at issue in the present case was not mentioned. The Supreme Court had for decades made use of a similar provision for refusing the admission of appeals under former Article 373 (3) no. 1 of the 1912 Code of Civil Procedure (see NOU 2001:32, p. 779). The High Court's role in appeal proceedings in a civil case was not to examine the case afresh but to review the first-instance court's decision that formed the subject of the appeal. It was sufficient that the High Court found it clear that the outcome would be upheld, possibly on a different reasoning than that given by the City Court (Ot.prp. nr. 51 (2004‑2005), p. 475). It was moreover a condition in Article 29-13 (5) that the three judges taking part in the decision to refuse admission to the appeal unanimously found that the appeal would not succeed (ibid., p. 476). Human Rights Committee considers that the lack of a duly reasoned judgment impairs the effective exercise of the right to have one’s conviction reviewed. The Norwegian Supreme Court, sitting in a Grand Chamber of eleven judges, delivered three decisions on 9 December 2008 (Norsk Retstidende – “Rt.” – 2008 at pp. 1764, 1783 and 1786) in criminal proceedings. It concluded that from Article 14 § 5 of the Covenant it followed that every High Court decision refusing admission of an appeal under Article 321 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure ought to be reasoned. The requirement of reasons was a necessary safeguard for ensuring a substantial review. The Supreme Court quashed a High Court decision refusing admission of an appeal on the basis of Article 29-13 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. A majority of seven members considered the subject matter in relation to Article 88 of the Constitution, according to which the Supreme Court was to adjudicate in final instance. The majority observed that this provision left the legislator great latitude in organising the national system of judicial remedies as it deemed appropriate. The extent of the reasoning required would vary considerably, depending on the nature of the particular case, ranging from a couple of sentences to more extensive reasoning of a legal or factual character. It would be insufficient to state the grounds for appeal and paraphrase the statutory requirement for refusing admission. Supreme Court’s competence to review the High Court procedure encompassed questions of whether a breach had occurred of expressly stated rules of procedure. The Supreme Court was empowered to fully examine the application of the law and the assessment of the evidence in relation to questions of procedure and, if necessary, determine whether an error of procedure had materialised. The majority said no constitutional obligation to give reasons for a High Court refusal to admit an appeal could be justified by the interests of the Supreme Court procedure. But the majority emphasised that, in. view of the points of law raised in the case, it was justifiable for the High. Court to refuse admission of the appeal. The Supreme Court’s majority found it unnecessary to consider the alternative plea that the decision had to be quashed in view of the requirements of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 14 of the Covenant. Two dissenting members disagreed with the majority view that the obligation to state reasons for a refusal of admission of an appeal in criminal cases also extended to civil cases. With effect from 10 December 2010, Article 29-13 (5) of the Code of Civil Procedure was amended to include a requirement that a refusal to admit an appeal under that article had to have been reasoned (“begrunnet”). For High Courts the financial and administrative consequences of the proposed changes should be manageable.

According to the applicants, Mr Kaba's exposure to asbestos at Hasköy Dock had caused his cancer. They were also concerned about the allegedly inadequate treatment he received at the GATA military hospital. The applicants also requested legal aid for the court fees. An officer in the Turkish Navy died of cancer in 2003. The applicants claimed that Mr Kaba's death was the result of the asbestos levels at Hasköy Dock and that he had not received adequate medical treatment at the GATA military hospital. They also requested legal aid for the court fees. The Military Supreme Administrative Court refused to grant the applicants legal aid, without giving any reason. On 22 April 2004 the applicants requested a rectification of the decision dated 21 January 2004. They were requested to pay the fees due within one month in order to be able to continue the proceedings. The application was denied and the applicants were told they would have to pay TRL 8,758,870,000 (approximately EUR 5,000) in court fees within a month.

Military Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the case on 12 May 2004. Decision was served on the applicants on 4 June 2004. Court also decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicants had not paid the necessary court fees. The decision dated 21 January 2004 was not a final decision on the merits of the case, a rectification or a clarification request was not possible under domestic law. decision dated 15 March 2004 was the final decision. Decision by the court was not appealed by the applicants. The case was eventually settled out of court in January 2006. The claim was dismissed due to a lack of proof of the severity of the asbestos at Hasköy Dock.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 1 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by the firm of F.M. Zumtobel. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30) and who was given leave by the President to use the German language. The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway, the L 52. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984. The authorities consulted several experts. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch. The Zumtobel partnership thereupon applied to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) It claimed that the expropriation proceedings, which were subject to final review, had violated its right of access to a court with full jurisdiction. The Office considered the first request to be irrelevant to the case; as to the second, it stated that the official expert had not shown any bias in favour of the authorities. The first applicant also challenged the decision of 13 February 1986 (see paragraph 10 above) in the Administrative Court. Relying on substantially the same arguments as in the Constitutional Court, it now complained of breaches of procedural and substantive law. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan was not enough to establish that the contested decision had been unlawful. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports. The court also rejected the complaints relating to the hearing of the official experts. The court considered that mere general remarks on the independence of official experts were not enough to prove a specific legitimate doubt. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the 1950 Law to doubt his complete impartiality. With reference to the complaints of lack of access to the case file, the court stated that it could not find that the Office had disregarded procedural rules, compliance with which could have led to a different decision. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it could also not claim a right to compensation. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS). In judging whether the decision-maker has exceeded this margin of appreciation the human rights context is important.
