The applicants’ challenge to the arguments in support of the policy was ‘completely persuasive’ However, the attack on the Secretary of State’s rationality fell ‘a long way short of success’ The policy was, in his view, “ripe for review and for consideration of its replacement by a strict conduct code’. The application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was rejected on 19 March 1996. In December 1997 Mr Beckett also issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming sexual discrimination contrary to the 1975 Act. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed.

eval_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. On 17 January 1998 the Commission decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court on the question of the applicability of the Council Directive on the Implementation of the Principle of Equal Treatment for Men and Women. The High Court granted Mr Beckett legal aid on 13 July 1998. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick and Mr Eadie. The hearing in this case and in the case of Smith and Grady v. the United Kingdom took place in public. The Circumstances of the case were heard by the Court in public at the Strasbourg Cour de cassation on 18 July 1999. The applications were declared admissible on 23 February 1998 and, while it retained the joinder of the present applications, it decided to disjoin them from the above-mentioned Smith and. Grady cases. The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. He became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy in 1983. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. He was involved in a steady relationship with a civilian partner. In early June 1994 he was informed that the Navy Special Investigations Branch (“the service police”) had been given his name anonymously in connection with an allegation of homosexuality and was investigating the matter. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. He then confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years’ service. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. On 16 December 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. The applicant was then called for interview by the service police. He was cautioned in the same terms as the first applicant and told that he would not be questioned on the above admissions prior to a search of his locker. The interview, which had lasted approximately five minutes, was suspended pending the search. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. Detailed questions were put as to how they had sex and whether they used condoms and lubrication. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett”. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) along with Ms Smith and Mr Grady obtained leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions to discharge them from the armed forces. Four men were discharged on the sole ground of sexual orientation. The High Court dismissed the application for judicial review. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He noted that the cases illustrated the hardships resulting from the absolute policy against homosexuals in the armed forces and that all four of the applicants had exemplary service records. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” Simon Brown LJ said even where the most fundamental human rights were being restricted, “the threshold of unreasonableness is not lowered” He said the courts owe a duty to remain within their constitutional bounds and not trespass beyond them. The Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and that the domestic courts could not rule on Convention matters. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the forces. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom’S obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to “management’s levels in the armed forces relating to the policy against homosexuals in those forces. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court of appeal agreed). The court may not interfere with the exercise of an administrative discretion on substantive grounds save where the court is satisfied that the decision is unreasonable in the sense that it is beyond the range of responses open to a reasonable decision- maker. But in judging whether the decision-maker has exceeded this margin of appreciation the human rights context is important. Master of the Rolls said the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind, that the decisions of which the applicants complained had had a profound effect on their careers and prospects and that the applicants’ rights as human beings were very much in issue. While the domestic court was not the primary decision-maker, “it has the constitutional role and duty of ensuring that the rights of citizens are not abused by the unlawful exercise of executive power,” he said. He concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights with which the primary adjudicating role on the Convention lay. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and, in particular, with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. The applicants’ arguments that their rights under Article 8 had been breached were “persuasive” but the evidence and arguments that would ultimately determine that issue were not before the Court Of Appeal. The applicants’ challenge to the arguments in support of the policy was ‘completely persuasive’ The policy was, in his view, “ripe for review and for consideration of its replacement by a strict conduct code’ Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Mr Beckett requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the. withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial. Tribunal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34129/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because, allegedly, the jury had been racially prejudiced. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The. applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59. § 1) of the case. The Court ruled that the application was not admissible as it was not part of the Convention.

The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because, allegedly, the jury had been racially prejudiced. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government of the United Kingdom and the applicant each filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The case was decided by the European Court of Justice on 28 June 1999.

The case originated in an application (no. 34129/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because, allegedly, the jury had been racially prejudiced. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. It was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court agreed the application was partially admissible and the Government filed written observations on the merits.

Juror complained that fellow jurors were 'making openly racist remarks and jokes' about Asians. The defence asked the judge to dismiss the jury on the ground that there was a real danger of bias. The judge decided to call the jury back into court, at which stage the juror who had written the complaint joined the others. The case has cost an enormous amount of money and I am not anxious to halt it at the moment, but I shall have no compunction in doing so if the situation demands. I am going to ask you all to search your conscience overnight and if you feel that you are not able to try this case solely on the evidence and find that you cannot put aside any prejudices you may have.

The case was adjourned after the judge asked the jurors to search their conscience overnight. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty of conspiracy to defraud. The judge said he would have no compunction in dismissing the jury if the situation demanded it. The juror was asked not to join the other jurors in the return of the case.

The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal on 1 March 1996. It would be unrealistic to suppose that the jury would not have wanted to know who the author of the complaint was and the judge dealt with the possibility of tensions among the jurors perfectly sensibly in the direction he gave them.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34129/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because, allegedly, the jury had been racially prejudiced. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits. By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The judge discussed the case and instructed the juror who had written the complaint not to join the other jurors. The case was settled out of court. The defence asked the judge to dismiss the jury on the ground that there was a real danger of bias. The judge called the jury back into court, at which stage the juror who had written the complaint joined the others. The next morning the judge received two letters from the jury. The first letter, which was signed by all the jurors, stated that we intend to reach a verdict solely according to the evidence and without racial bias. A second letter was written by a Juror who appeared to have thought himself to have been the one who had been making the jokes. The juror in question explained at length that he might have done so, that he was sorry if he had given any offence. The judge decided that he would not discharge the jury and told them the following: “Ladies and gentlemen, the events of yesterday afternoon were clearly distressing for you, but I am sure you will see and realise that when a judge receives a note from one of your number raising those sort of issues it is the judge's duty to bring it to the attention of the whole jury.” On 8 March 1995 the jury found the applicant guilty, but acquitted G.C., who was also Asian. On 20 April 1995 the judge imposed on the applicant a sentence of five years' imprisonment. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal on 1 March 1996. Judge dealt with the possibility of tensions among the jurors perfectly sensibly in the direction he gave to them. However, it would be unrealistic to suppose that the jury would not have wanted to know who the author of the complaint was. Other members of the jury, as this led to his identification, were also asked to identify themselves. The jury was unable to reach a verdict on the case because of the nature of the complainant's injuries. The case was adjourned until next week at the earliest. The trial will resume on Friday at the High Court in London. The verdicts are expected to be returned in the next few days and the jury will be sequestered.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the Swedish courts’ protracted custody proceedings violated Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Hague Convention. The application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section of the Court. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The case was decided in favour of the applicant and his right to have his daughter returned to him. The case has been decided in favor of the Swedish Government and the application was dismissed. The decision was made by the President of the Third Section.

The case originated in an application (no. 3684/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the Swedish courts’ protracted custody proceedings violated Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Hague Convention. On 1 February 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section. The application was decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time (Article 29 § 1).

The case originated in an application (no. 3684/07) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by R. Harrold-Claesson, a lawyer practising in Olofstorp. The Swedish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Sjöberg, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time.

In 1999 the applicant married L., a Ukrainian national holding permanent residence permits in the Czech Republic and in Sweden. In August 2003 their daughter, N., was born. L. visited her parents in Prague together with N. between May and August 2005. Upon their return, the applicant’s relationship with L. quickly deteriorated and, in September 2005, she returned to her parents’ home in Prague. They have remained there ever since. The court found that neither the applicant nor L. appeared to be unsuitable as guardians for N. Therefore, despite their difficulties in co-operating and the distance between their places of residence, there were not enough reasons to dissolve the joint custody.

The case involves a Swedish woman and her Czech daughter. The applicant asked for joint custody of their daughter but wanted contact rights on a regular basis. The court ruled in favour of the applicant and ordered an investigation into the custody of N., her place of residence and contact to her. The case was heard at the District Court (tingsrätten) in Kristianstad, Sweden, in November 2005. It was decided that N. should live with her mother and see her father for four hours every other weekend in the presence of L. or a person of her choice. The application was dismissed on appeal on October 25, 2006.

The applicant married a Ukrainian national in 1999. In August 2003 their daughter, N., was born. The applicant submitted an application for divorce from L. in September 2005. He also requested sole custody of N. or, if the court decided that the parties should have joint custody, that N. should live with him. L. agreed to the divorce but opposed the applicant’s requests in relation to their daughter. She wanted sole custody but agreed, pending the final outcome of the proceedings, that the applicant could visit N. in Prague for a few hours every other weekend with her or her mother present. The court found that neither the applicant nor L. appeared to be unsuitable as guardians for N.

The case was taken to the Court of Appeal of Skåne and Blekinge. L. moved to Prague, which made it more difficult for N. to see her father. The court found it was in the child’s best interest to live with L. even though L. had made it harder for N to see him. The Social Council made an investigation concerning the custody of N., her place of residence and the contact rights. No appeal lay against the decision, and the case was decided in favour of L. in December 2005. In February 2006, the court rejected the appeal, noting that it was not legally possible to decide where a child should live; it could only decide with whom.

The applicant requested the District Court to change its interim decision, inter alia, in respect of N.’s place of residence and the contact rights. He claimed that the interim decision in force had made it impossible for him to create meaningful contact with N. The Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. No appeal lay against the decision. The parties were left to agree on where it would be best for N. and the applicant to meet. The application was rejected on the grounds that it was not legally possible for it to decide where a child should live; it could only decide with whom. N. is now living with her father in Sweden.

The Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Skåne and Blekinge upheld the lower court’s decision in full. The parties were left to agree on where it would be best for N. and the applicant to meet. In 2006 the Social Council made an investigation concerning the custody of N., her place of residence and the contact rights. L. wanted his right of contact with N. to be exercised in southern Sweden. N. had a great responsibility to ensure that N. would be able to see the applicant. L., by moving to Prague, had made it more difficult for N to see her father.

The District Court mandated a company, Access Borders SE, to investigate N’s living conditions in the Czech Republic. The report was to be submitted to the court at the latest on 15 October 2007. The court decided that N. should meet with the applicant for four hours on 8 December 2007 and for four. hours on 9 December 2007 in Sweden. The hearing was cancelled and, apparently, the applicant and N. did not therefore meet as scheduled. The District Court decided that L. should have the sole custody of N. and granted the applicant a right of contact with N. four days in a row on a monthly basis.

The court decided that N. should meet with the applicant for four hours on 8 December 2007 and for 4 hours on 9 December 2007 in Sweden. The date for the main hearing in the case was fixed for 11 and 12 December 2007. But the hearing was cancelled and, apparently, the applicant and N. did not therefore meet as scheduled. On 27 July 2010 the District Court, after having held an oral hearing, delivered its judgment. It decided that L. should have the sole custody of N. and granted the applicant a right of contact with N. four days in a row.

The court decided that N. should meet with the applicant for four hours on 8 December 2007 and for 4 hours on 9 December 2007 in Sweden. The date for the main hearing in the case was fixed for 11 and 12 December 2007. However, the hearing was cancelled and, apparently, the applicant and N. did not therefore meet as scheduled. On 27 July 2010 the District Court decided that L. should have the sole custody of N. and granted the applicant a right of contact with N. four days in a row.

The applicant applied to the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs for assistance for the return of N. in accordance with the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (‘the Hague Convention’) The application was forwarded to the District Court in Kristianstad since the latter was dealing with the custody case. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal, which refused leave to appeal on 29 September 2010. On 8 December 2010 the Supreme Court refused leave. to appeal. The appeal was rejected and the case is now pending in the European Court of Human Rights. The case is currently being heard by the International Court of Justice.

In December 2005 the applicant applied to the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs for assistance for the return of N. to Sweden in accordance with the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (‘the Hague Convention’) The application was forwarded to its Czech counterpart. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal, which refused leave to appeal on 29 September 2010. On 8 December 2010 the Supreme Court refused left to appeal. The court held that, despite invitations from L., the applicant had not even once gone to Prague. The advantages of a change of N’s domicile would not outweigh the drawbacks, inter alia, since N. had not seen the applicant for several years and no longer spoke Swedish.

In December 2005 the applicant applied to the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs for assistance for the return of N. in accordance with the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (“the Hague Convention”) The Ministry for. Foreign Affairs, which is the Swedish Central Authority in charge of matters falling under the. Hague Convention, forwarded the applicant’s request to its Czech counterpart. In June 2006 the. Ministry for foreign Affairs forwarded this request to the District Court in Kristianstad since. the latter was dealing with the custody case. In October 2006 the District. Court declared that L.’S retention of N in the Czech Republic was not unlawful within the meaning of Article. 3 of the Hague. Convention. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court.

The applicant opposed the change of N’s place of residence in the Swedish population register (folkbokföringen) since he considered the removal of N. to be unlawful and the custody proceedings were still ongoing. The applicant applied to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) for re-opening of the case as he considered that he had suffered a miscarriage of justice. The Supreme Court rejected the application on 1 February 2007. N. no longer lived at the registered address in Sweden but with L. in Prague since 10 September 2005. The Tax Authority removed N. from the population register as having emigrated.

L. sent a notification of change of address to the Swedish Tax Authority (Skatteverket) on N.’s behalf. The applicant opposed the change of N’'s place of residence in the Swedish population register (folkbokföringen) since he considered the removal of N. to be unlawful and the custody proceedings were still ongoing. The Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's appeal, finding that neither the removal nor the retention of N by L. by L was unlawful. This judgment was final. However, the applicant applied to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) for re-opening of the case as he considered that he had suffered a miscarriage of justice. The Supreme Court rejected the application.

In 2006 L. sent a notification of change of address to the Swedish Tax Authority (Skatteverket) on N.’s behalf. Since parents who have joint custody of a child need to agree on a change of. address for the child, the Tax Authority forwarded the notification to the applicant for comments. The applicant opposed the change of N.'s place of residence in the Swedish population register (folkbokföringen) since he considered the. removal of N to be unlawful and the custody proceedings were still ongoing. On 19 December 2006 the Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's appeal, finding that neither the removal nor the retention of N by L. by L was unlawful. This judgment was final.

The Supreme Court of Norway refused to accept the appeal against the decision of the European Court of Human Rights. The case is still being heard by the Court of Justice of the EU. The court ruled that the decision to reject the appeal was a breach of the right of the Court to consider the appeal on the merits. The Court of Appeal said that the appeal should be rejected as it was not in the public interest to hear the case on its own. The decision was made to stop the appeal until the appeal could be heard on a full hearing. The Supreme Court said that it had no power to refuse the appeal because it was a matter of international law.

The Supreme Court of Sweden refused leave to appeal the decision. The decision was made under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Supreme Court ruled that the decision was based on the merits of the case, not on the principle that it should be decided by the court. The case is still pending before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France. The judge ruled that it was a breach of the Convention's Article 13, which states that it is the right of the court to consider a case on a case-by-case basis. The court made the decision on the basis of the merits, not the fact that the case had already been decided by a court of law.

The Supreme Court of Sweden has refused to allow the case to proceed. The judge said that the case should be dealt with on the merits, not as a result of the court's decision. He added that the appeal should be heard on the grounds of the law of the land, not the case of the case itself. The appeal was made in the Supreme Court under Article 13 of the Convention, which protects the right of the public to have a voice in the case. The case is now being heard by the High Court of Justice of Sweden, which is expected to make a decision on the appeal in the next few days.

The decision on the admissibility and merits of the application was made at the same time (Article 29 § 1) as the decision on whether or not to rule on the merits. L. agreed to the divorce but opposed the applicant’s requests in relation to their daughter. She wanted sole custody of N. but agreed, pending the final outcome of the proceedings, that the applicant could visit N. in Prague for a few hours every other weekend with her or her mother (N.'s maternal grandmother) present. In its interim decision, the court noted that neither the applicant nor L. appeared to be unsuitable as guardians for N. L. appealed against the decision to the Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Skåne and Blekinge, maintaining his requests for sole custody and for her to live with him. In the alternative, he wanted his right of contact with N to be exercised in southern Sweden. The applicant requested the District Court to change its interim decision, inter alia, in respect of N’s place of residence and the contact rights. He claimed that the interim decision in force had made it impossible for him to create meaningful contact with N. The Court of Appeal rejected the appeal, noting that it was not legally possible for it to decide where a child should live; it could only decide with whom. The court found it to be in the best interests of N. to keep the interim arrangements until final judgment was delivered in the case. The hearing was cancelled and the applicant and N. did not therefore meet as scheduled in Sweden. L. took a number of procedural decisions, inter alia, rejecting L.’s request to have all documents in the case-file translated into Czech and deciding that the parties should finalise their pleadings by 21 April 2008 so that the main hearing could take place. The court decided that L. should have the sole custody of N. and granted the applicant a right of contact with N. four days in a row on a monthly basis, which should gradually be increased. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal, which refused leave to appeal on 29 September 2010. On 8 December 2010 the Supreme Court refused leave. to appeal. Later decisions by the Swedish courts could not justify the removal retroactively. In November 2005 L. sent a notification of change of address to the Swedish Tax Authority (Skatteverket) on N.’s behalf. Since parents who have joint custody of a child need to agree on a change. of address for the child, the Tax Authority was called on to sign off on the change. The applicant opposed the change of N’s place of residence in the Swedish population register (folkbokföringen) since he considered the removal of N. to be unlawful and the custody proceedings were still ongoing. The applicant lodged a further appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten), maintaining his claims and invoking Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. He considered that since the custody case and the proceedings relating to his demand under the Hague Convention were still pending, the Tax Authority should not prejudge those proceedings by removing N. from the population register as having emigrated. The Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Gothenburg refused leave to appeal.

At a distance of 28 miles from Cape Finisterre it sent out an SOS after sustaining sudden and severe damage which produced a leak. The spillage of the ship’s cargo caused an ecological disaster whose effects on marine flora and fauna lasted for several months. The shores of the Atlantic coast of Cantabria and Galicia were severely polluted by the numerous waves of oil which were washed up. The oil spill blackened beaches and cliffs, destroyed marine life, adversely affected water quality and had an immediate environmental impact on numerous animal species.

The Court considers it useful to outline the circumstances under which the parliamentary elections of 22 July 2007 took place. In early May 2007 the Turkish Parliament decided to hold early parliamentary elections. The decision followed a political crisis resulting from Parliament’s inability to elect a new President of the Republic to follow on from Ahmet Necdet Sezer before the expiry of his single seven-year term of office. Fourteen political parties took part in the elections, which were marked by two characteristics. A strong mobilisation of the electorate was observed following the presidential crisis, since the participation rate rose to 84%. Political parties used two pre-electoral strategies to circumvent the national 10% threshold. More than sixty independent candidates stood for election in about forty provincial constituencies.

He was charged by his CO, pursuant to section 70 of the Army Act 1955 (“the 1955 Act”), with indecent assault contrary to section 14(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. It appears that his two co-accused were charged with rape. On the same date, the CO referred the case to a higher authority and remanded the applicant in close arrest.

Six ‘16-day arrest’ forms were also completed (pursuant to Rule 22 of the Investigation and Summary Dealing (Army) Regulations 1997) on 19 November, 3 December and 20 December 1999 and on 4 January, 20 January and 7 February 2000. The CO of the MCTC signed these forms and recorded that the applicant had been brought before him to consider any representations the applicant may have had concerning his arrest status and that he had been informed of his right to apply to the military authorities for his release. No representations from the applicant were recorded as having been made. No reasons were noted as to why the applicant was detained except in the last form which recorded the same reasons as in the above-noted 8-day reports: “He is likely to suborn witnesses”

On 12 January 2000 a solicitor was instructed by the applicant's parents. On 13 January 2000 that solicitor took instructions from the applicant. eval_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand pending his trial by court martial was in breach of Article 5 § 3 of the treaty. By a decision of 25 October 2005, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The case was heard by a Chamber of the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) on 24-25 October 2005. A certificate dated 6 November 1999 and signed by the applicant confirms that the applicant received the pamphlet “The Rights of a Soldier Charged with an Offence under the Army Act 1955” On the same date, the CO referred the case to the Higher Authority and remanded the applicant in close arrest. A short note by the CO (“referred to Higher Authority”) constitutes the sole record before the Court of that hearing. The final report dated 7 February 2000 recorded for the first time an additional charge against the applicant pursuant to section 70 of the 1955 Act: rape contrary to section 1(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. No reasons were noted as to why the applicant had been detained except in the last form (dated 7 February 2000) which recorded the same reasons as in the above-noted 8-day reports. “He is likely to suborn witnesses. Having regard to the nature or prevalence of the offence under investigation it is undesirable in the interests of discipline that he should be at large or consort with his comrades.” The applicant's representative applied for a writ of habeas corpus to the High Court. The application was served on the CO of the MCTC on 19 February 2000. On 22 February 2000 the applicant was released from close arrest and he was posted to the 47th Regiment Royal Artillery. The applicant and his two co-defendants were tried by Army General Court Martial on a joint charge of rape between 14 May and 25 May 2001. All three defendants were acquitted. I decided that the Applicant should be posted with immediate effect to a different unit in a different country namely the UK, and issued with specific orders preventing him from being able to influence the witnesses. He was released into open arrest even though the allegation against him was that he had committed rape and indecent assault...and despite the fact that there was evidence that he, with others, concocted a story and interfered with a witness. The applicant was placed under house arrest for six months.

In his petition to the Court of Cassation he complained about the loss that he had suffered as a result of the high rate of inflation during the proceedings before the civil court. On 23 July 2001 the applicant was paid the total amount of TRL 282,795,000, consisting of the capital plus interest incurred until the payment date. The amount was paid out over a period of seven years, starting on 17 July 1989 and ending on 1 January 2000. The total amount paid to the applicant for the additional work was TRL 287,938,000. It was calculated at the rate of 30% per annum running from 17 July1989 to 1 January 1998; 50% perannum from 1 January1998 to 1 April 2000; and at the rediscount rate running from 1 February 2000 until the date of payment.

The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was made on 17 May 2005 by a Polish national, Mr Jan Kachel (‘the applicant’), who is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment. On 16 April 2003 the applicant was indicted on a charge of murder allegedly committed with two accomplices, who were also on trial. The courts repeatedly justified the applicant’s pre‑trial detention in the initial phase by the existence of strong evidence against him. On 4 July 2005 the Katowice Regional Court convicted the applicant and his co‑defendants as charged. The applicant was sentenced to 25 years’ imprisonment. The prosecutor and the lawyers of all three defendants lodged appeals. On 8 November 2006 the Supreme Court dismissed a cassation appeal lodged by the applicant. The appeal was dismissed on 25 January 2006. The Supreme Court upheld the substance of the first‑instance judgment concerning the characterisation of the charges and the sentence.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21906/09) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a period of ten years, which had been the maximum for such detention under the legal provisions applicable at the time of his offence, violated Article 5. The application was initially represented by Ms M. Kronfeldner, his sister, and subsequently by Mr A. Ahmed, a lawyer practising in Munich. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin. Regensburg Regional Court convicted the applicant of rape. It sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment and ordered his placement in preventive detention. The court found that in July 1989, some four months after his release from prison, the applicant had raped a woman whom he had come across in Regensburg at night. The applicant had previously been convicted, in addition to several offences against the property of others, of attempted rape committed in 1973, two counts of sexual assault committed in 1978 and rape and coercion committed in 1984. On 25 October 2007 the Regensberg Regional Court prolonged the execution of the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital. The Regensburg Regional Court considered that it was very likely that the applicant, if released, would commit further serious offences resulting in considerable physical or psychological harm to the victims. The court quashed its decision of 26 October 2005 to execute the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital and decided to retransfer the applicant to prison in accordance with Article 67a § 3 of the Criminal Code. On 22 July 2008 the Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of the Regional Court. The applicant was accordingly transferred from Straubing Psychiatric Hospital toStraubing Prison on 19 June 2008. The case was heard by the Court of Appeals in Berlin and the decision was appealed to the Supreme Court of Germany. The Court of Appeal, fully endorsing the reasons given by the Regional Court, dismissed the applicant’s appeal as ill‑founded. The psychiatric expert report drawn up by expert K. was clear and conclusive and complied with the minimum standards required for such reports. The court further referred to the leading judgment dated 5 February 2004 of the Federal Constitutional Court, in which the latter had considered the retroactive extension of a convicted person's preventive detention beyond a period of ten years to be constitutional. It found, accordingly, that the applicant's continued preventive detention was lawful and proportionate. The case was settled in November 2008. The applicant remains in preventive detention in Straubing Prison. The applicant was considered by Straubing Prison authorities to be a self-confident, demanding and mistrustful person. He consistently refused the treatment offered, questioning the therapists’ expertise. He was not granted any relaxations in the execution of the preventive detention order against him for fear of abuse. Since July 2009 he has been working in the prison’s furniture factory. The applicant did not make any of the therapies available – notably a group or possibly individual social therapy for sexual offenders – for lack of motivation. The Federal Court of Justice decided to adjourn the case pending a decision of its grand senate on the legal question at issue. It remitted the case-file to the Nuremberg Court of Appeal to review whether, applying a stricter standard of proportionality, the applicant's preventive detention was to continue. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of the Regensburg Regional Court of 26 July 2010. It found that, having regard to the criteria set up by the Federal Constitutional Court in its judgment dated 4 May 2011, the applicant’s preventive detention was disproportionate. It had not been shown that the applicant, owing to specific circumstances, was highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. The applicant had not previously been placed in a psychiatric hospital under section 1 of the Bavarian (Mentally Ill Persons’) Placement Act (see paragraph 39 below). The applicant was transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital thereupon. The court ordered preventive detention in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years’ imprisonment and if the following further conditions are satisfied. The court may review at any time whether the further execution of the preventive detention order should be suspended and a measure of probation applied or whether it should be declared terminated. For persons in preventive detention, the time‑limit is two years (paragraph 2 of Article 67e). The first period of preventive detention may not exceed ten years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3). Article 67d of the Criminal Code was amended by the Combating of Sexual Offences and Other Dangerous Offences Act of 26 January 1998. The detention of mentally ill persons is provided for, first of all, in the Criminal Code as a measure of correction and prevention if the detention is ordered in relation to an unlawful act committed by the person concerned. The detention of a person with diminished criminal responsibility can also be ordered to be placed in a psychiatric hospital if a comprehensive assessment of the defendant and his acts reveals that, as a result of his condition, he can be expected to commit serious unlawful acts and that he is therefore a danger. The court may quash that decision if it later emerges that no success can be achieved by placing the person in a. psychiatric hospital or a detoxification facility (Article 67a § 3) A court may order a person’s placement in a psychiatric hospital at the request of the authorities of a town or county if the person concerned is mentally ill and thereby poses a severe threat to public security and order. Such an order may only be executed as long as no measure under Article 63 of the Criminal Code has been taken. Recent case-law of the Federal Constitutional Court on preventive detention has allowed such an order to be carried out. The person concerned has been found guilty by final judgment of certain serious offences for which preventive detention may be ordered under Article 66 § 3 of the criminal Code. He must further suffer from a mental disorder owing to which it is highly likely that he will considerably impair the life, physical integrity, personal liberty or sexual self-determination of another person. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty. These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal Code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. The court ruled that the courts dealing with the execution of sentences had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. The Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention. It stressed, in particular, that the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment required an individualised and intensified offer of therapy and care to the persons concerned. In line with the Court’s findings in the case of M. v. Germany, it was necessary to provide a high level of care by a team of multi-disciplinary staff. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. On 19 September 2011 the Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. Under Article 173 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozessordnung – hereinafter ‘the CCP’) a court was only allowed to conduct minor enquiries to fill in remaining gaps in an investigation. The Federal Constitutional Court (hereinafter ‘the Constitutional Court’) refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted. In its decision the Constitutional Court referred to the case-law concerning the procedural obligation of Article 2 of the Convention and, in particular, to the cases of McCann and Others v the United Kingdom.

It appears from the submitted tax return forms concerning SEDNO’s business for January to October 2002 that the applicant made an eight-digit gross profit and a seven-digit net profit in that period. The court further considered that this in itself justified the refusal to exempt him from court fees as he could have put money aside for that purpose.” The applicant applied for compensation of PLN 545,918.65 and asked to be exempted from court fees. The Koszalin District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) declared the applicant’s company insolvent on 3 December 2003. The Gdańsk Court of Appeal gave a decision exempting the applicant from any fees exceeding PLN 10,000 (approx. EUR 2,500) on 14 May 2004. The court considered that the court fee of PLn 28,896 had to be reduced to PLN 14,000. The decision was rejected on the basis that the presiding judge had not signed the decision of 19 November 2003. Koszalin Regional Court ordered the applicant to pay a court fee of PLN 10,000 for lodging his statement of claim on pain of having it returned. The court further found that, while it was true that the applicant was in debt and that his tax return for the period from January to October 2003 had shown a loss in the amount ofPLN 68,538.74 (approx. Two men went on trial on charges of importing and supplying controlled drugs. The proceedings were relayed through a closed-circuit television system to a remote viewing room in the court building. On 23 September 2004, it was discovered that police officers and prosecution staff had been watching the proceedings. The trial judge took the decision to desert the trial diet simpliciter since he believed that no fair trial could continue before him. This decision had the effect of bringing the prosecution case to an end resulting in the acquittal of the accused. The appeal was scheduled to be heard by the High Court of Justiciary (sitting as an appeal court in Edinburgh) on 15 February 2005.

The trial judge made an interim order under section 4(2) of the Contempt of Court Act 1981 preventing the publication of any report of the proceedings. The Crown appealed against the decision of the trial judge to desert the trial diet simpliciter. The appeal was scheduled to be heard on 15 February 2005. The High Court made an order prohibiting the publication of a report of any part of an appeal hearing until completion of the appeal. The order was to become final on 17 February 2005 unless an application was made to recall or vary it. On the afternoon of 15 February 2005, BBC Scotland sent another fax to the High Court stating that it wished to be heard on the order as soon as possible. The Government maintain that BBC Scotland did not contest the decision not to hold a hearing before 18 February 2005. The Appeal Court deferred its consideration of BBC Scotland's application for the recall of the section 4(2) order until 21 June 2005.

On the same date, the appeal court deferred its consideration of BBC Scotland's application for the recall of the section 4(2) order. Two men went on trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting at Glasgow on charges of importing and supplying controlled drugs on 13 September 2004. The proceedings were filmed and relayed through a closed-circuit television system to a remote viewing room in the court building. On 23 September 2004, it was discovered that police officers and prosecution staff had been watching the proceedings with the risk that defence conversations might have been overheard. This decision had the effect of bringing the prosecution case to an end resulting in the acquittal of the accused. The Crown appealed against the decision of the trial judge to desert the trial diet simpliciter. The appeal was scheduled to be heard by the High Court of Justiciary (sitting as an appeal court in Edinburgh) on 15 February 2005. The High Court made a section 4(2) order prohibiting the publication of a report of any part of the appeal hearing until the appeal was completed. The Government, in their observations to this Court, maintain that BBC Scotland did not challenge that decision. The order was posted on the Scottish Courts Service website and circulated to the Scottish media. BBC Scotland sent a number of letters to the Clerk of the High. Court of. Justiciary, seeking an opportunity to address the court should an application to prevent. publication of any report of the appeals proceedings be made. The Government maintain that BBC Scotland did not contest the decision not to hold a hearing before 18 February 2005. The applicants maintain that their fax of 15 February 2005 was intended to be an application to recall or vary the interim order. If the High Court dismissed the prosecution's appeal, then BBC Scotland would be heard by the court in respect of the section 4(2) order. On 21 June 2005, the Appeal Court recalled that order. The Appeal Court deferred its consideration of BBC Scotland's application for the recall of the sections 4(3) and 4(4) order until the appeal was heard on 17 March 2005. On the same date, the appeal court recalled the order of the trial judge and substituted an order for desertion pro loco et tempore.

In November 2008, the applicant lodged a request. for revision with the Federal. Court. The Federal Court upheld the request for revision and annulled its judgment of 3 May. 2004, limiting the duration of the applicant’s exclusion to ten years from 2 June 2003. The European Court found that, in view of the circumstances, and particularly of the applicant’s relatively serious convictions, the weakness of his links with his country of origin, and the permanent nature of the removal measure, Switzerland had failed to strike a fair balance between the interests (private and public) at stake. It specifically emphasised that the indefinite duration of the exclusion had been ‘particularly harsh’, taking the view that the possibility for the applicant to have the exclusion order suspended temporarily or permanently rescinded remained purely speculative at present. This is the principle of restitutio in integrum, which has the practical effect of limiting the freedom of States in the choice of means to remedy a violation of the Convention. The applicant’s links with Turkey were at that time weaker than those he enjoyed with Switzerland, such that a return to his country of origin appeared to be a relatively harsh measure for him. In those circumstances, it was not possible for the applicant's private interest in remaining in Switzerland to prevail over the public interest in his expulsion. The only appropriate solution in order to alleviate the effects of the impugned measure against the deportee would consist in limiting the duration of the exclusion. 4.3 Consequently, it is justified to limit the removal measure ordered against the applicant to a period of ten years with effect from the removal decision of 2 June 2003. After such time he will be able to lodge an application for leave to remain, which will be examined by the European Court of Human Rights. On 11 September 2009 the applicant married a German national. As a result of that marriage he has obtained a German residence permit. On 19 April 2010 he lodged with the Administrative Court for the Canton of Neuchâtel an application for reconsideration of a decision of 27 December 2005. In a judgment of 20 August 2010, the court rejected the request and referred the matter back to the Immigration Authority. The response to his request for the revocation of the removal measure so that he could settle in Switzerland was negative. The right to family reunification is always predicated on the existence of original leave to remain granted to an EC/EFTA national under the provisions of the ALCP. The applicant appealed to the Courts-Martial Appeal Court, which had the power to quash the conviction if it considered it unsafe. Lord Chief Justice, Lord Bingham of Cornhill, gave judgment on 30 July 1996, dismissing the appeal. 'With the benefit of hindsight, it seems plain that the trial could have been conducted in England without undue difficulty,' he said. 'It would in our view have been preferable if this young appellant, whose subjection to military law was purely vicarious and involuntary, had been tried here with all the procedural safeguards which procedure in the ordinary criminal courts affords'

The trial of a young civilian by court-martial was inherently unfair and oppressive and thus an abuse of process. The atmosphere in a military court would be very different from that of a civilian court and the applicant would not do himself justice. Had the appellant been held in Germany to await trial, as he could have been, his claim to trial in England would have appeared weaker. If tried by jury, a majority of 10 to 2 votes would be necessary to convict him, whereas a simple majority vote would suffice in a trial by court martial. The Lord Chief Justice, Lord Bingham of Cornhill, gave judgment on 30 July 1996.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40426/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention about his trial by court-martial. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The case was adjourned pending the judgment of the Grand Chamber in Grieves v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 57067/00, ECHR 2003‑XII. The parties each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits of the complaints. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicant was living with his family in Germany, where his father was an Army Corporal serving in the Support Unit of the Rhine Garrison. On 8 February 1994 the applicant was charged with the murder of a young civilian woman. The German authorities waived jurisdiction pursuant to the NATO Status of Forces Agreement 1951. The applicant returned to England in April 1994 where he was detained. His father was discharged from the army in November 1994. He was returned to Germany in time for his court-martial which commenced on 21 April 1995. The Court of Appeal held that the trial was inherently unfair and oppressive and thus an abuse of process. The judge said: “The atmosphere in a military court would be very different from that of a civilian court and the atmosphere in the courtroom would be different as well’ The trial ended with the applicant’s conviction on 3 May 1995. In accordance with the provisions of the Army Act 1995, the verdict of the court-martial was confirmed by a Confirming Officer. The applicant appealed to the Courts-Martial Appeal Court, which had the power to quash the conviction if it considered it unsafe. The Lord Chief Justice, Lord Bingham of Cornhill, giving judgment on 30 July 1996, held, dismissing the appeal: “... We have some considerable sympathy with the appellant's complaint.” The appeal court certified a question of law for law for the applicant to appeal. The applicant was convicted of the murder of a German soldier in Germany in 1997. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, who dismissed the appeal. The court-martial was held under section 209 of the Army Act 1955. The application was dismissed on the grounds that proceedings in accordance with the 1955 Act could be considered abusive. The appeal was dismissed by the Lords on 16 December 1997, and the case was dismissed again on 9 July 1997, after the applicant's appeal had been granted leave to appeal. 'It seems to me that the legislation was enacted to ensure that the grave offences with which it deals should not go unpunished when committed abroad by a British citizen,' said Lord Hope. Many of the witnesses were German and could not be forced to attend a trial in England. There were 13 German witnesses who could be divided into three categories. The defence had not yet indicated what evidence would be agreed. The Director of Public Prosecutions would have had to take his decision well before the trial, in view of the arrangements which would have to have been made for the appellant to be transferred into the hands of the civil authorities in England and for the attendance of witnesses. No agreement was reached, despite several written requests and reminders, about any of the evidence until the commencement of the trial when the evidence was agreed piecemeal during the opening days. There is no sound basis for thinking that, at the time when a decision about this would have had to have been taken, a prosecution in the English courts within a reasonable time would have been seen to be practicable. The alternatives lay between taking proceedings by way of court-martial in Germany, leaving the matter in the hands of the German public prosecutor or taking no proceedings at all. ... Conclusion ... The proceedings were conducted within the rules laid down by Parliament. ...” “There was no case to answer”, said the lawyer. “We are satisfied that the decision to take no proceedings was the right one.” Trial of those who have ceased to be subject to military law is expressly provided for by section 131 of the Act. Since the Armed Forces Act 1976, where a civilian defendant is to be tried, civilian Crown servants can be detailed as members of the court-martial. Most criminal offences allegedly committed by a civilian dependent would be tried by a Standing Civilian Court (similar to a Magistrates’ Court), with trial by court-Martial reserved for the most serious offences. From 1 April 1997 (after the conclusion of the applicant’s court- Martial) the Armed forces Act 1996 came into force which modified certain provisions of the Army Act 1955 (see, generally, Cooper v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 48843/99, ECHR 3003-XII). The basic rule of the common law is that the jurisdiction of the criminal courts in the United Kingdom is confined to crimes committed within the territory of each court. An exception is provided by section 9 of the 1861 Act, which gives jurisdiction to British courts in respect of alleged murders and manslaughters committed by British citizens anywhere in the world. The Offences against the Person Act 1861 gives British courts jurisdiction over alleged murders in any part of the world (see ECHR 2003-XII). According to the ECHR, the law applies to all people in the UK regardless of where they live, with the exception of criminals in the U.S. and Canada.

The applicant complained that the decision was arbitrary and breached her right to peaceful enjoyment of her property. She submitted that Section 112 of the Medical Practitioners Act, which allowed for exemption from the liability to pay contributions to the pension and invalidity fund, did not sufficiently allow for private initiatives in ensuring an adequate pension. A preliminary ruling on that issue should be obtained by the European Court, she said. The case was referred back to the Appeal Committee, which dismissed the appeal on 15 October 2003. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint on 27 February 2004 without holding a public hearing. In the 1950s the Irish Free State was under the control of the Catholic Church. The system was set up so that the Church could have control of primary schools. The Irish Constitution was changed in 1998 to give the State control of schools. But the system was still largely controlled by the Church in the early 1960s. The provision of free primary education was made part of the Constitution, but the role of the church was largely limited to the day-to-day running of the schools. It was only after the Act was passed that the role was made more clearly defined and the Church was given more control over the school system. The issue of child protection was also a factor in the decision to change the system.

In the early 20th century, Ireland had a number of Catholic schools. They were under the control of the Catholic Church. When the Irish Free State was formed, they were managed by the Church. This was in line with the role of the Church in Ireland. The Catholic Church was responsible for managing the schools. The provision of free primary education was not until 1998 that it was made a statutory duty. In the 1950s, there were about 3,000 schools in the country. The Church had control of about half of the schools, the rest were run by non-Catholics. The rules for the schools were laid out in 1965, but they were not very detailed.

Dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State. Hardiman J noted that, in recent times and after more than a century and a half, the provision of education was belatedly placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Hardiman J concluded that the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. In particular, even applying the wider form of vicarious liability invoked, the Minister’s absence of direct control over L.H., long since ceded to the manager and the patron, prevented a finding against the Minister. The relationship of L.h. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church” – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland's unique historical experience. The manager was the agent not of the Minister, but of the Catholic Church, the power in whose interest the Minister was displaced from the management of the school. Hardiman J: The Minister was simply providing assistance and subvention to private and corporate (i.e. Roman Catholic) endeavour, leaving the running of the school to the private or corporate entities. Kenny J: In my view the Constitution specifically envisages, not indeed a delegation but a ceding of the actual running of schools to the interests represented by the patron and the manager. Fennelly J: Cases of sexual abuse had preoccupied the criminal courts and the Supreme Court for many years and it was surprising that that court was confronted for the first time with questions relating to the liability of institutions including the State for sexual abuse of schoolchildren. Fennelly J accepted the expert’s evidence that it was not a State system but rather a ‘State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) He concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint to the State. Geoghegan J dissented. He accepted that neither the Department nor its inspectors had any knowledge of the assaults. He considered that, for all practical purposes, most primary education in Ireland took the form of a joint enterprise between Church and State. The Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid. The judge noted that if an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. If the police found the complaint justified, the teacher’s licence to teach could be withdrawn.

The applicant was charged with wounding with intent and also with attempting to pervert the course of justice by telling the police that he had seen two black men stab S. When witnesses were questioned at the scene, no-one claimed to have seen the applicant stabbed S. Two days later, however, one of the witnesses, T., made a statement to police saying he saw the applicant stab S., but it is clear that he did not see who stabbed him. Prosecution argued under the CJA 2003 that T. was too fearful to attend trial before the jury and that he should qualify for special measures. The trial judge heard evidence from a police officer conducting the case who testified that the Iranian community was close-knit and that T.'s fear was genuine. T. himself gave evidence to the judge from behind a screen. In ruling that leave should be given for the statement to be read to the jury, the trial judge stated: “I am satisfied in those circumstances upon the criminal standard of proof that this witness is genuinely in fear’. The judge said he was satisfied that the defendant’s evidence, if he chooses to give it, would be sufficient to rebut and to challenge the evidence. T.'s witness statement was read to the jury in his absence. The judge warned the jury about the danger of relying on the evidence of T. The applicant was convicted by a majority verdict, principally of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. He was later sentenced to nine years' imprisonment to be served concurrently with a term of fifteen months' imprisonment for doing an act intended to pervert the course of justice. The Court of Appeal acknowledged, however, that the Crown accepted that T.'s statement was “both important and probative of a major issue in the case...and had it not been admitted the prospect of a conviction would have receded” Court of Appeal held that the jury was informed of all matters necessary to its decision-making process. The applicant's sentence was reduced to seven years' imprisonment. Leave to appeal on conviction was refused on 24 January 2006. It was ruled that the trial judge had explicitly warned the jury in detail as to how they should treat this evidence and properly directed them as tohow they should consider it in reaching their verdict. The application was rejected on 26 January 2006, and the appeal was dismissed on 25 January 2006 and the applicant was sentenced to six years in prison. The appeal was denied on 2 February 2006, with the sentence reduced from six years to seven.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2034/07) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the decision of the Supreme Court finding him guilty of serious insult against the King of Spain amounted to an unjustified infringement of his right to freedom of expression. In view of the information available to it, the Court decided that no hearing was necessary. The application was lodged by a Spanish national, Mr Arnaldo Otegi Mondragon (‘the applicant’), on 5 January 2007. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Blasco, Head of the Legal Department for Human Rights, Ministry of Justice. The Basque Country High Court of Justice had jurisdiction to try the applicant because of his status as a member of parliament. The public prosecutor lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant for “serious insult against the King’Within the meaning of Article 490 § 3 of the Criminal Code read in conjunction with Article 208, on account of his remarks made on 26 February 2003. The applicant argued that his remarks had constituted political criticism directed against the Head of the government of theBasque Country. The criminal proceedings in the Basques Country High court of Justice took place on 7 April 2003. He was found guilty of insulting the King and sentenced to two years in prison. In a judgment of 18 March 2005, the High Court of Justice found the applicant not guilty of the charges against him. After stating that his remarks had been “clearly offensive, improper, unjust, ignominious and divorced from reality’, the court found as follows: “... This is not an issue concerning the private life of the Head of State but one of rejection of the ties of political power deriving from the hereditary nature of the institution which he personally symbolises’“. The Constitution does not guarantee the right to freedom of expression solely in relation to certain points of view that are considered correct, but in. relation to all ideas, subject to the limits which it lays down ...” The public prosecutor lodged an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court. He argued that the law protected the honour of the King as a specific individual possessed of personal dignity. In the view of the public prosecutor, it was clear that the King had been performing official duties and that he was a figure in the public eye. That did not deprive him of the right to respect for his honour. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the lower court, making several references to the Court's case-law. It sentenced the applicant to one year’s imprisonment, suspended his right to stand for election for the duration of the sentence and ordered him to pay a fine. The Supreme Court considers the impugned remarks to have been value judgments rather than statements of fact. Judge P.A.I. issued a dissenting opinion in which he argued that the comments complained of had been of a political nature. The judge agreed with the Basque Country High Court of Justice that the remarks had not targeted the King’s private life or his personal honour but had been directed solely at his institutional role as Commander-in-Chief of the Spanish armed forces. The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court alleging, inter alia, a breach of his right to freedom of expression (Article 20 § 1 (a) The Supreme Court’s judgment had incorrectly weighed the competing interests at stake. The statements in question had not been disproportionate in the context in which they had been uttered. The Constitutional Court noted at the outset that the right to freedom of expression did not encompass a right to proffer insults. It pointed out in that connection that the Constitution did not prohibit the use of hurtful expressions in all circumstances. However, freedom of speech did not protect vexatious expressions which, regardless of their veracity, were offensive and ignominious and were not pertinent for the purpose of conveying the opinions or information in question. The Court considered that the weighing of the competing rights at stake had been carried out in an appropriate manner by the Supreme Court. The King occupied a neutral position in political debate. This implied that he was owed institutional respect of a kind that was ‘substantively’ different from that due to other State institutions. The Constitutional Court held that the applicant’s remarks, on account of their obviously derogatory nature, had clearly gone beyond what could be considered legitimate. The applicant was imprisoned on 8 June 2007 after the Supreme Court upheld a judgment of the Audiencia Nacional of 27 April 2006 sentencing him to fifteen months’ imprisonment for publicly defending terrorism. According to the Government, his sentence was remitted on 16 July 2009. He is currently in pre-trial detention in connection with other criminal proceedings.

London Clubs Limited (“LCL”) owned and controlled six of the twenty casinos licensed to operate in London. In June 1991 a raid took place at the various premises of LCL. In March 1992 the Gaming Board lodged objections with the clerk to the Licensing Magistrates with regard to LCL's annual application for renewal of its licences. The Gaming Board also made cancellation applications in respect of the existing licences held by LCL and a meeting was held. As a result of that meeting, the applicant and the other executive directors (with the exception of the finance director) resigned with effect from 30 April 1992, on the understanding that such resignation was involuntary and constituted dismissal by London Clubs.

Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. On 10 October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report, he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear (unklare Verkehrslage). The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. He was given a fine of DM 125, to which were added costs of DM 14, for “joint responsibility for a road crash due to overtaking in an unclear traffic situation such that a collision was caused’.
