Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. On 10 October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act and Regulations 1(2), 5 and 49 of the Regulations. The applicant was fined DM 125, to which were added costs of DM 14.

Road Traffic Regulations (Strassenverkehrs- Ordnung) read: “All road-users have a duty to conduct themselves in such a manner as not to harm or jeopardise others or inconvenience or annoy them more than may be inevitable in the circumstances“ Regulation 5 provides that motorists must overtake on the left (paragraph 1), that they may overtake only if they can see that they will not thereby interfere with oncoming traffic (paragraph 2) and that no overtaking is allowed in an unclear traffic situation (paragraph 3(1)). By Regulation 49(1)(1) and 49(5), it is a “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) to contravene Regulations 1(2) and 5(1), and such an offence is punishable by a fine.

The driver of the car was likewise fined for a ‘regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) The proceedings were stayed on the ground that they were time-barred. The costs of the proceedings shall be borne by the Treasury (Staatskasse) The defendant shall bear his own necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) The court ruled that the driver had to pay the costs of his own prosecution. The court also ruled that he would not have to pay costs if he had not breached the Road Traffic Regulations (Strassenverkehrs- Ordnung) The decision was made on 9 December 1980.

The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence’ The court told the applicant that it intended to discontinue the proceedings as they were time-barred and order costs against the Treasury (Staatskasse) The applicant would have to bear his own necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) On 12 August, Mr. Wingerter replied that his client naturally agreed to the stay of proceedings. The costs of the proceedings shall be borne by the Treasury. The defendant shall be required to pay his own costs. The trial was held in Heilbronn.

Heilbronn Police Authority took a decision to impose a fine (Bussgeldbescheid) on the defendant for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. The defendant appealed against this decision. The court declines to order the Treasury to bear the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury. The decision on costs is based on Article 467 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, taken together with section 46 of the Act on ‘regulatory offences’ (Gesetz über Ordnungswidrigkeiten) (see paragraph 19 below) The court held that Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) of the Convention did not apply to the case. As it had already explained at length in an earlier decision, Article 6 protected the individual only from possible hazards.

Heilbronn Police Authority took a decision to impose a fine (Bussgeldbescheid) on the defendant for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. The defendant appealed against this decision. Prosecution of the ‘regulatory offence’ became time-barred under section 26(4) of Road Traffic Act. In accordance with Article 206a of the Code of Criminal Procedure, taken together with section 46 of the Act on ‘Regulatory offences’, the court declines to order the Treasury to bear the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury. The court held that Article 6 of the Convention did not apply to the case.

Heilbronn Police Authority took a decision to impose a fine (Bussgeldbescheid) on the defendant for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. The defendant appealed against this decision. Prosecution of the ‘regulatory offence’ became time-barred under section 26(4) of Road Traffic Act. In accordance with Article 206a of the Code of Criminal Procedure, taken together with section 46 of the Act on 'regulatory offences', the court declines to order the Treasury to bear the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses. The court held that Article 6 (art. 6) protected the individual only from possible hazards in civil or criminal trials.

Mr. Lutz applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) but was turned down. The court held that Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) was not applicable because it could not apply to proceedings in connection with “regulatory offences’ These had been excluded from the category of criminal offences, and procedure relating to them was quite distinct from criminal procedure. Mr Lutz had thus broken the basic rule in Regulation 1(2) of the Road Traffic Regulations and, in particular, had disregarded his duty under Regulation 5(3)(1) not to overtake where the traffic situation was unclear.

Mr. Lutz had himself admitted to the police that he was not expecting the car which was moving out to the left onto the road in front of him to make a U-turn. He had consequently attempted to overtake it but had been unable to avoid a collision despite his efforts to brake. The court held that in such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury, especially as the prosecution had become time-barred only during the court proceedings. The possibility of conversion into a custodial sentence makes no difference, since conversion is possible only in the event of the appellant’s refusing to pay the fine out of sheer unwillingness.

He said that he had intended to obtain a high-school diploma and then go on to study communication science at university with an eye to becoming a journalist. In his view the new selection system tended to direct holders of diplomas from such vocational schools into two-year technical training programmes in higher technical colleges (Meslek Yüksek Okulu), graduates from which could not aspire to executive posts in the media.

The case was heard by the European Court of Justice in Strasbourg on 15 October 2007. The applicant is Jarosław Kąkol (“the applicant”), a Polish national, born in 1969 and lives in Gdynia. The trial began on 28 December 2001. The bill of indictment listed 120 charges brought against 19 defendants, who were all detained on remand. The case file comprised 114 volumes. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses. The trial court ordered the removal of the applicant and two other defendants from the court room. The Court of Appeal instructed the trial court to hold more than 3 hearings per month. The Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's requests for the presiding judge to withdraw from the trial. The application was dismissed on 11 September 2002 and the trial was adjourned until 30 September 2002. However, as of 22 April 2002 the reading out of the bill of indictments had still not been concluded. The applicant and his 17 co-defendants were ordered to be kept in custody until 30 June 2003. The Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's request for the judges and lay members of the trial court to withdraw. The Court of Appeal ruled that the detention was justified under Article 258 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure since that provision established a presumption to the effect that the likelihood of a severe penalty being imposed on the applicant might induce him to obstruct the proceedings. In addition, it observed that the trial could not have been terminated due to obstructiveness on the part of the defendants who had filed numerous requests. The applicant was jailed after being accused of being a member of an organised criminal group. The Court of Appeal ordered his continued detention until 31 March 2005. In its decision of 27 July 2005 dismissing the applicant's appeal against the decision of 22 June 2005 prolonging his detention, the Court of appeal referred, inter alia, to the presumption established under Article 258 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It also held that keeping the applicant in custody was necessary in order to prevent him from interfering with the trial, given the reasonable risk of such interference which flowed from the fact that he had been charged with commission of offences. By March 2006 the trial court had held some 135 hearings of the 162 which had been scheduled. The case began in March 2005 but no hearing was held due to the serious illness of the judge rapporteur. On 21 September 2005 the President of the IV Criminal Section of the Gdańsk Regional Court assigned a new judge. Consequently, the trial had to commence de novo. On 18 October 2005 a different panel of the Court of Appeal quashed the impugned decision and ordered the applicant's release under police supervision. The applicant was released on 19 October 2005. It appears that the proceedings are still pending before the first-instance court. The trial court made a further severance order and divided the case into eleven separate cases on 24 November 2005.

They also requested an interim measure to stay their deportation under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. On 8 January 2008 the request was refused. The applicants did not pursue their application. On 6 February 2008, a Committee of three judges decided to strike it out of the Court’s list of cases. The proceedings giving rise to the present application include the Immigration Appeals Board's decisions of 31 August 2007 and 31 May 2005 on the two applicants. In September 2007 the applicants challenged that decision before the courts. In this connection they both requested an interlocutory injunction to stop their deportation. These requests were rejected by the City Court on 5 October 2007 and the High Court on 15 November 2007. By a judgment of 4 February 2008, the Oslo City Court quashed the Immigration Appeals Board’s decision of 31 August 2007, disagreeing with the Board's assessment that the applicants lacked special attachment to Norway. The City Court further observed that in Norway the applicants had close relatives – uncles and aunts – and had lived with these since 2001. The applicants had gone to school in Norway, had friends and acquaintances there and were mastering the Norwegian language. The applicants had not had contact with their father since 1996 and did not wish to have any contact with him. Their mother had died and it was uncertain whether they had other relatives in the country. They were able to speak Urdu and to understand the language in oral form but could not read or write it. The High Court found it clear that the refusal to grant residence permits constituted an interference with the applicants’ rights under paragraph 1 of Article 8 of the Convention. The State appealed to the Borgarting High Court, which overturned the City Court’s ruling by a judgment of 14 November 2008 and upheld the Immigration Appeals Board's refusal of 31 August 2007 as being lawful. The High Court found it hardly probable that the applicants had no contacts with their mother and had no knowledge of her whereabouts from 2001 until the summer of 2005. It was difficult to ascribe any responsibility to the applicants for not having taken any steps to leave the country while the mother had gone into hiding from the police. After reaching the age of majority, the applicants’ choice to stay in Norway had been something for which they ought to bear the risk and responsibility. There were generally speaking strong immigration policy considerations in favour of identifying children with the conduct of their parents. If it were to be otherwise, there would be a great risk that parents exploited the situation of their children to secure a residence permit. The applicants had developed a strong personal and social attachment to Norway. They had received the essential part of their education and upbringing there. The High Court, nonetheless, arrived at the conclusion that the refusal of residence had not been unlawful as being contrary to Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It was rare that one was confronted with cases where the duration of the unlawful stay had been nearly as long as in the present case. One could therefore question whether general immigration policy considerations, which normally carried weight in cases of unlawful residence, would be sufficiently weighty to regard the refused of residence as being ‘necessary in a democratic society’ The Supreme Court refused the applicants leave to appeal. It attached decisive weight to the fact that the applicants’ strong attachment to Norway had been established during unlawful residence. No new circumstances had occurred between the two decisions of 31 May 2005 and 31 August 2007 (see paragraphs 11 and 17 above) that could warrant a different conclusion than that reached by the High Court in its judgment of 13 October 2006 (see paragraph 14 above). The Immigration Appeals Board decided to stay the implementation of the applicants in June 2010. The applicants took refuge in Holmlia Church, Oslo, in the summer of 2009. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5786/08) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Swedish State had failed to comply with its obligation to provide her with remedies against her stepfather’s violation of her personal integrity. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 21 June 2012 a Chamber composed of Dean Spielmann, President, Elisabet Fura, Karel Jungwiert, Mark Villiger, Ann Power-Forde, Ganna Yudkivska, André Potocki, delivered its judgment. The applicant was 14 when she discovered that her stepfather had hidden a video-camera in the laundry basket in the bathroom, which was in recording mode and directed towards the spot where she had undressed before taking a shower. Immediately after the incident, the film was burned without anyone seeing it. In 2005 the public prosecutor indicted the applicant’s stepfather for sexual molestation (sexuell) The applicant was born in 1987 and lives in Ludvika. The Government each filed further observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Human Rights Centre of Ghent University had been granted leave by the President of the Grand Chamber to intervene in the written procedure. The applicant, her stepfather, her mother and her cousin gave evidence before the District Court of Falun (Falu Tingsrätt) The applicant’s stepfather explained that he had lived with her mother from 1997 until the autumn of 2003. They had separated on account of the incident in question, among other things. He had wanted to try to film with a hidden camera, but it had been an impulsive act. He was not sure whether the camera had been in recording mode or whether a film had been recorded. The applicant's mother had burned the film without her seeing it. She had not reported the incident to the police until 2004, when she heard that the applicant's cousin had also experienced incidents with the accused. The District Court convicted the applicant’s stepfather on all four counts of sexual molestation under Chapter 6, Article 7 § 3, of the Penal Code. The Court of Appeal acquitted him on the counts ofsexual molestation allegedly committed against the applicant. The applicant was given a suspended sentence combined with seventy-five hours’ compulsory community service. The stepfather was ordered to pay the applicant damages in the amount of SEK 20,000. The judge said he had had a sexual intention in hiding the camera in the laundry basket and directing it at the part of the bathroom where it was usual to undress. The buzzing sound from the camera heard by the applicant strongly suggested that the camera was switched on and was actually recording. Man was acquitted of sexual molestation because he had not intended his girlfriend to find out about the filming. Supreme Court held that the isolated act of filming was not a crime in itself. In Swedish law there was no general prohibition against filming an individual without his or her consent. The Court of Appeal went on to point out that the act might, at least theoretically, have constituted the crime of attempted child pornography (försök till barnpornografibrott) considering the applicant’s age. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8658/79) lodged with the Commission on 18 June 1979 by Mr. Helmut Bönisch, a German national. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Austria recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany advised the Registrar, on 30 July 1984, that her Government did not intend to participate in the proceedings. The applicant, on the other hand, stated that he wished to participate and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. G. Wiarda. President Wiarda had asked the Government to suspend execution of fines imposed on Mr. Bönisch. Mr. Evrigenis and Mr. García de Enterría were prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case. Mr J. Cremona and Mr R. Bernhardt, substitute judges, were appointed as substitute judges. The hearing was adjourned until 21 January 1985. The Court of Justice heard evidence from both sides and ruled in favour of the applicant. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and to the Court of Appeal (ESH) for further proceedings. The ECHR ruled that the case should be sent back to the Austrian courts. The hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. Immediately before they opened, the Court had held a preparatory meeting. The Court heard addresses and replies to its questions from Mr. Türk, Mrs. Kabelka and Mr Lindner for the Government, Mr. Schermers for the Commission and Mr. Roessler for the applicant. The various speakers also produced to the Court several documents. The applicant lodged three further documents on 19 February. The application was made by a citizen of the Federal Republic of Germany born in 1936. He runs a firm that specialises in meat smoking. The maximum quantity permissible in smoked meats of a carcinogenic substance called benzopyrene 3.4 was stated to be one part per (American) billion. In October 1976, the Market Office of the City of Vienna drew two samples of smoked meat from the production of the Bönisch company. The Institute was entrusted with carrying out the analysis of these samples. In its analysis, the Institute found a benzopyrene concentration of 2.7 and 3.0 ppb respectively and an excessive water content. The samples were therefore described as being dangerous to health and adulterated. This opinion by the Institute, which had been drafted on 28 November 1976, amounted to the lodging of a complaint. The case came before the same judge of the Regional Court who in 1976 had dealt with an earlier case against the applicant (see paragraph 9 above) The judge and the expert took part in the proceedings. Mr. Bönisch, who was not represented by a lawyer, stated that a water content below 1.8 per cent was technically unattainable and requested the hearing of a meat and sausage expert. The Regional Court however refused this, on the ground that black smoking was forbidden if the water content could not be limited to the required level. In a judgment delivered the same day (29 June 1978), the Regional Court found the applicant guilty of offences under section 56(1), nos. 1 and 2, and section 63(1) of the German Food Code. Mr. Bönisch appealed. He took issue with the Director of the Institute for not having adhered to the opinion of his colleagues. He also raised objections of principle against the appointment as court expert of the very person who had reported the case to the prosecuting authorities. The Vienna Court of Appeal rejected the appeal on 19 December 1978. As to the carcinogenic effects of benzopyrene, it noted that the Regional Court had based its decision on the opinions of the Medical Faculty, which, according to settled case-law, could not be contested. Apart from that, the regional Court had extensively dealt with all relevant aspects of the case before holding that the products made by the applicant were adulterated and dangerous to health. The Institute once more found an excessive concentration of benzopyrene (6.1 ppb) and an undeclared high water-content. Criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant before the Vienna Regional Court. The case came before the same judge who again appointed the Director of the Institute as expert pursuant to section 48 of the 1975 Act. On the same day (20 September 1979), the Regional Court found the applicant guilty of offences against sections 56 and 63 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal ruled out the hearing of a counter-expert since the expert opinion obtained in the first-instance proceedings was not tainted with any defects. Mr. Bönisch appealed from this decision on grounds similar to those pleaded in the first proceedings (see paragraph 14 above) The Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 20 May 1980. On 28 February 1984, the Federal President, exercising his power to grant a pardon, commuted the two prison sentences imposed on the applicant to fines of 30,000 and 15,000 Schillings (see paragraphs 13 and 17 above). The 1975 Act provides that the Market Office of a city shall periodically draw samples of foodstuffs and send them for analysis to the Institute. This expert must possess special professional qualifications and have a special authorisation from the Federal Ministry of Health (sections 47 and 50) Section 48 of the 1975 Act involves a derogation from the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure in so far as expert evidence is concerned. Under Article 120 of the said Code, the prosecuting authorities and the accused are to be informed of the names of the experts appointed by the court. If any doubts persist or if the findings of these experts ‘are unclear, vague, contradictory’, the court may call another expert. Under the terms of Article 149 of the same Code, only the prosecutor and the defence counsel are entitled to put questions to witnesses and experts. Witnesses, on the contrary, do not have this possibility. The matter was debated in Parliament prior to the passing of the Act and subsequently in 1978 when a proposed amendment to section 48 was examined. This amendment, which was not in fact adopted, provided that both the Institute’s expert and any private expert called by the accused were to be heard only as witnesses. The receipt by Institute officials of certain bonus payments also gave rise to some discussion which subsequently provoked their discontinuance. The Commission expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a breach of Article 6 para. 3 (d) (art. 6-3-d) in the first proceedings. The full text of the Commission's opinion is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1249/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that a number of police officers had subjected him to ill-treatment and that the national authorities had not only failed to carry out an effective investigation, but had also failed to punish those responsible. On 10 May 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention). The applicant threw stones at the police officers and kicked and punched them, injuring one of them in the process. He was taken to the First Aid Hospital in Istanbul’s Taksim district where a medical report was prepared. The same day the prosecutor referred the applicant to the Beyoğlu branch of the Forensic Medicine Institute where he was examined by a doctor. The prosecutor rendered a decision of non-jurisdiction, under the Law on the Trial of Civil Servants, and transferred the case file to the governor's office for the “necessary action to be taken” The applicant was then brought to the office of the public prosecutor and released. Three police officers were convicted of the offence of ill-treatment contrary to Article 245 of the Criminal Code. The trial court reduced the prison sentences by a quarter and sentenced each officer to two months and seven days’ imprisonment. Two of the three police officers lodged appeals against the judgment. The judgment became final in so far as it concerned the third police officer, who did not appeal. The Court of Cassation held that the provisions of Law no. 4616 should be applied to the two police officers. The sentences were suspended under Article 6 of law no. 647 of the Turkish Criminal Code, which provides for the suspension of criminal cases in respect of certain offences. On 28 May 2002 the Beyoğlu Assize Court rejected the applicant’s objection. Nevertheless, the fact remained that the ill-treatment to which he had been subjected constituted “torture” within the meaning of the United Nations Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. The trial court had no choice but to apply Article 245 of the Criminal Code in the present case. In accordance with Article 245, the trial court was required to rule that the alleged victim had been mistreated in a ‘degrading and cruel’ way. The court ruled that the defendant had been treated in such a way in violation of Article 245.

The case involves a dispute over 728,000 old Polish zlotys. In July 1984 the plaintiff died and his wife and daughter joined the proceedings as his legal successors. The case was heard in February 1989, and the plaintiffs again modified their claim in 1989. In November 1992 the court obtained fresh expert evidence in order to determine the value of certain construction works made by the second applicant. In August 1996 the court decided to obtain new expert evidence to determine value of the land on which the hen house had been constructed. On 12 November 1996 the expert report was submitted to the court. On 11 December 1996 the case was adjourned until later that year. The applicants requested that the court index the repayment of their bank loan and the payment made to the original plaintiff in 1984. The applicants also requested to obtain documentary evidence from the land register. The court fixed a one-month time-limit for the parties to produce the evidence. On 26 March 1998 the court gave judgment. It partly granted the claim of the original. plaintiff’s daughter against the second applicant and dismissed the claim. of the first applicant. None of the parties submitted a notice of appeal. The case had been assigned to a new judge. It did not obtain any expert report even though the applicants had secured money for such a report.

Özmen, Co-Agent, Mr H. Ünler, Ms Z.G. Acar, Ms E. Esin, Ms D. Kilislioğlu, and Mr S. Duman, Advisers. Alevism is a belief or philosophy influenced by other cultures, religions and philosophies. It represents one of the most widespread faiths in Turkey after the Hanafite branch of Islam. It advocates close contact with nature, tolerance, modesty and love for one's neighbour, within the Islamic faith. Alevis reject the sharia (code of laws in orthodox Islam) and the sunna (forms of behaviour and formal rules of orthodox Islam). They believe that Allah is present in each person and that Allah created Adam in his image. According to Alevism, Allah is neither in the sky nor in paradise, but in the centre of the human heart. The Turkish government has been trying to force schools to teach religious culture and ethics. The move is in breach of the law, which states that religious education is part of the curriculum. The Turkish government is trying to get the law changed to make religious education optional for children. A court has ruled that the law should remain as it is, and that teaching religious culture is a matter for the schools to decide. The court has also ruled that it is not illegal to teach religion in a primary or high school, as long as the teacher is a member of the community and the student is from that community. The school can only teach religious education if it is a compulsory subject, and can't teach it in any other way.

The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1) In support of his application to postpone enforcement regarding the sale of movable property, the debtor claimed he would risk losing his property rights over the objects seized for enforcement. The applicants were not notified of the appeal. The Steyr Regional Court (Landesgericht) quashed the decision, ordering both kinds of enforcement to be postponed until the decision on the action under Section 35 of the Enforcement Act was rendered and re-setting the deposit at EUR 1,000. It held that an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court was not admissible and the applicants were obliged to reimburse legal costs amounting to EUR 305.40 to the debtor.

The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below). In accordance with the relevant legislation, an inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. The Commission produced to the Court the documents in the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. Inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture. (13) The buildings would have led any reasonable person to have concluded that he or she was looking at the start of a small new detached housing estate.” The buildings lie in part of the green belt but outside the village policy area for Higher Whitley. They did not look as if they had been designed for the purposes of agriculture. My opinion is not altered by my finding them now being used for storing hay. The use of domestic-style eaves and gable barge boarding. The residential look of the ‘porch’ to No. 1 building. And the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food’s. view about the uneconomic layout of both buildings as originally built all add. to the impression that these buildings were not designed for agricultural purposes. “The applicant appealed against this decision under section 289 TCPA (see paragraph 24 below). In his Notice of Motion, the applicant first alleged that the inspector had “erred in law in applying the wrong test in deciding whether the buildings were permitted development”. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order’. In my judgment ... it cannot be said that. the inspector failed to take into account the fact that the applicant might, within his General. Development Order rights, erect buildings of a broadly similar nature. He addressed that very consideration in terms at paragraph 15. Inspector extended the applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h) because the applicant had those rights and wanted more time to erect a replacement or replacements. Whether the existence of these General Development Order rights provided sufficient reason for the inspector to grant planning permission for the buildings in fact erected, whether or not conditioned as suggested by the applicant, was a matter for judgment - the inspector's judgment. Whether another decision-maker would have reached the same conclusion as did this inspector is not to the point. Nor is the view of this court, which does not sit on appeal from the judgment of inspectors, relevant. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.

The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 18 November 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), and the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The parties replied to the Court in writing. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. The applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal, and his substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, against the Registrar's decision of 27 January 1994, was dismissed on 2 May 1995. The defendants were ordered to serve their evidence by 17 January 1997. They failed to do so. The case was adjourned until March 1998. They were allowed to serve more evidence before the case was dismissed. The hearing was settled by the Court of Appeal on 25 April 1998. The decision was not appealed by the defendants. The court ruled that the case should be dismissed as it was not in the public interest to hear the other side's evidence. It was dismissed and the case against the defendants was dismissed on 14 June 1998. This was followed by an extension of time for the defendants to give further evidence. The final hearing was held on 9 February 1998 and the decision was upheld. The applicant applied for a five-year disqualification period. The Secretary of State agreed to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement. In March 1998 the time-limit for the applicant’s further evidence was extended indefinitely. On 30 June 1999 the Secretary of state informed the applicant that he had decided not to discontinue them. The trial was set down to begin on 4 October 1999. The application for leave to apply for judicial review was refused. The applicant renewed his judicial review application before the Court of Appeal. On 23 March 2000 Buxton LJ refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. In the course of a considered judgment, Lord Justice Buxton described the application as ‘misconceived’. Human Rights Act 1998 came into force on 2 October 2000. On 10 November 2000 the applicant issued an application in the Companies Court to strike out or dismiss the disqualification proceedings. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal refusing leave to apply for judicial review. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissed it on 15 February 2001. In Re Blackspur Group [1998] 1 WLR 422, 427H and 433B it was recorded that Mr Davies did not suggest then that a fair trial was impossible. A very large proportion of the undoubtedly long time which has elapsed since these proceedings were commenced is due to the various actions taken by Mr Eastaway. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of MrEastaway’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them.

She immediately identifies the security officer in a photo. In their minutes the police officers at times refer to Elaine B. not by her name but as ‘the nigger woman’ She is repeatedly linked to prostitution. For the first interview in the interview room no trained interpreter can be found. The traumatised woman is initially interviewed by a man. His statement, like that of the victim, is disregarded. Disturbing errors occur. Elaine B. denies this version of events. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. If she had really been hoping to be granted asylum, why would she then have defamed the security officer? Next to take the witness stand are the employees of the bakery. Saleswoman R.Z.: ‘She gave him a kiss. She was fairly young, I’d say between 20 and 25. I couldn’t describe the woman’ When confronted with Elaine B. a few days before. She had stroked his back and ‘cosied up’ to him. No evidence is taken either from other asylum seekers or from the female staff in the women’s quarters. Judge I.K. acquits the security officer. The reasoning is diametrically opposed to that of the Court of Appeal. ‘It cannot be established that the accused performed sexual intercourse against the will of Elaine B. be made out beyond doubt’, states the judgment. According to the court, the bakery employees could not have identified Elaine. The ‘black African’ on the other hand, appeared ‘very confident’ with the result that ‘it is hard to imagine that she could have felt so intimidated by the accused’ Judge I.K. had no doubt about the woman’s guilt. The judge ignored relevant evidence and delivered a scandalous judgment. Justice Minister K.M. has promised to do more to protect the victims of crime. She should study this case. Elaine B. must appear before the investigating judge ‘or be brought by force’ She could face up to five years in prison. ‘That’'s just routine, nothing unusual’ says a Justice Ministry spokesman. According to principal public prosecutor P.: ‘After [the] acquittal we have no choice but to initiate proceedings’ The compensation proceedings under the Media Act are under way. In October 2005 the applicant company sought the disqualification of Judge N.F., the judge assigned to the media proceedings, for bias. It considered that by publishing the impugned statements it had merely expressed criticism, protected by the freedom of speech. The president of the Vienna Regional Court dismissed the motion on 17 October 2005 and held that the issue raised by the applicant was not sufficient to give rise to doubt that the judge would not decide the case objectively. On 12 December 2005 the Regional Court held another hearing in the defamation proceedings in which it examined two of the witnesses proposed by the applicants. The third witness proposed did not appear. The Regional Court found that the contents of the article had given a biased account of the taking of evidence at the trial of H.P. I.K. was therefore entitled to compensation, which it set at 7,000 euros (EUR) It also ordered the applicant company to publish a summary of the judgment. According to the article, the judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced, whereas the rape asserted by K. had been described as proven and the assessment of evidence by the Regional Court as absurd. Such an account was not an objective critique of the Judgment, the court found. The Regional Court found that the applicant company had not succeeded in proving the truth of the impugned statements. The accusation that a judge, who was under the duty to act objectively and impartially, had deliberately disregarded evidence in order to acquit an accused from the same country had to be qualified as defamation. An error in the translation of that statement could not be excluded, but that did not allow the conclusion that there had been no basis in the file for the above finding. The term scandal of justice was a value judgement, which, however, was based on assertions of fact which had been disproven in the proceedings. The Regional Court found that the amount of EUR 7,000 in compensation was appropriate. The applicant company appealed on 8 March 2006 against the Regional Court’s judgment. On 19 June 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment. This judgment was served on the applicant’S company lawyer on 29 June 2006. The judge said the judge's critique of Judge I.K. in the impugned article, which had lacked any sufficient factual basis, had been excessive. He added that the judge had been wrong to criticise the judge in the first place and that he had been right to condemn the judge for his actions.

The German Criminal Code distinguishes between penalties and measures of correction and prevention. The sentencing court may, at the time of the offender's conviction, order his preventive detention under certain circumstances in addition to his prison sentence if the offender has been shown to be dangerous to the public. In particular, the sentencing court orders preventive detention in. addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years' imprisonment and if the following further conditions are satisfied.

The order for execution of the placement in preventive detention must be met by three conditions. The perpetrator must previously have served a prison sentence or have been detained pursuant to a measure of correction and prevention for at least two years. A comprehensive assessment of the perpetrator and his acts must reveal that, owing to his propensity to commit serious offences, the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. The court responsible for the execution of sentences must review, before completion of the prison term, whether the person's preventive detention is still necessary in view of its objective. On 21 August 1997 she lodged a preliminary claim with the Valencia Council, which she relied on Article 15 (right to life and to physical integrity) The applicant sought 3,907 euros (650,000 pesetas) for the damage she had sustained and the cost of installing double glazing. The Valencia High Court of Justice dismissed the application for judicial review. The Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal admissible and summoned the parties to a hearing on the merits on 16 May 2001. The applicant repeated her factual and legal submissions, stressing that there had been a violation of her rights to life, physical and mental integrity, privacy and the inviolability of the home. The case was settled by a Spanish jury in October 2002. The verdict was upheld by Spain’s Supreme Court. The Valencia City Council raised a number of preliminary objections to the appeal. It argued that there was no evidence of noise levels inside the applicant’s home and that the authority concerned should not bear sole responsibility for the noise to which the applicant had allegedly been exposed. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2001, which was served on 29 May 2001. It ruled that the amparo appeal was hybrid in nature, that is to say that it alleged a violation of Articles 15 and 18 § 2 of the Constitution by the City Council and a breach of Articles 14 and 24 by the Valencia High Court of Justice. The appeal was dismissed after also dismissing the city council's preliminary objections. The Constitutional Court found that the applicant had not established a direct link between the noise and the damage she had sustained. The court also found that there was no evidence of any violation of Articles 14 and 24 of the Constitution. The applicant's allegation that the judgment did not contain sufficient reasons could not be regarded as arbitrary or unreasonable, the court found. The European Court of Human Rights had held that, in cases of exceptional gravity, repeated damage to the environment could infringe the right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 § 1 of the Convention, even if did not endanger health. The Constitutional Court held that that test had not been satisfied in the case before it and pointed out that the only evidence she has adduced is a certificate stating that she was admitted to hospital and saw a doctor. The Constitutional Court dismissed the amparo appeal on the following ground: “Consequently, as regards the alleged violation of the rights relied on, the appeal must be dismissed, as the appellant has failed to prove the existence of a genuine effective breach of fundamental rights attributable to the Valencia City Council” Two judges expressed concurring opinions. The first said that the judgment restricted the free development of the personality at home. The second judge pointed out in his concurring opinion that there was a preliminary problem that had not been adequately dealt with, namely the degree to which the relevant authority was required to provide the requested protection. The authorities were obliged to exercise their power when the breach of the fundamental rights attained a certain level of gravity.

The applicant suffered from serious rheumatism which necessitated her to move continuously and was in a poor mental condition. Her detention in Braunschweig Police Station, with little possibility to move, had already led to her joints having stiffened. The applicant's small cell, equipped with a mattress and a chair, was lighted at least via a ventilation slot and by electric light. She went outside for a walk on the banks of the Ilmenau river with the police officers three times during that period. The places and conditions of the applicant’s detention in the Lüneburg Police Station from 7 p.m. onwards until 7 November 2008 at approximately 1.40 p.M. The applicant was detained in the Braunschweig Police Station from 8 November 2008. Her cell was equipped with a bed, an empty desk, a chair and an open cupboard and had a barred window with frosted glass. The applicant had climbed on the cupboard in her cell and passed the night thereon, failing to comply with the police’s order to descend. On 15 July 2009 the Lüneburg District Court dismissed the applicant's action of 8 November2008 under section 19 § 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. The proceedings for review of the lawfulness of the applicant’re detention and of the conditions thereof are set out below. The District Court confirmed that the detention had complied with section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. The photographs of shackled persons exposed in the detention wing of the Braunschweig Police Station may have been tasteless, but did not render the applicant’s detention unlawful as a result of intimidation. The recommendations of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) were irrelevant here. The applicant's complaint that her detention cells did not have windows, but only ventilation slots, was considered to be without merit. The fact that the light had remained switched on all night in Braunshweig had been a consequence of the applicant's own behaviour. The Lüneburg Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 July 2009. The court ruled that the conditions of the applicant’‘onerous’ detention had complied with the applicable legal provisions and had not been so unacceptable as to render the execution of her detention unlawful. The judge also found that the doctor who visited the applicant in detention and had persuaded the then competent District Court judge to order her release had probably been a sympathiser. The Regional Court said that the cell in which the applicant was held was uncomfortable, but complied with no. 15.1 of the Police Custody Regulations in the version then in force. The Regional Court noted that the applicant arrived at that station on 8 November 2008 at 2.10 a.m. after the crew of the ambulance called by the police and a police doctor had confirmed her fitness for detention despite the breathing difficulties she had informed the police of. The court considered that it had been lawful for the police to leave the light switched on during the night. Shackling the applicant to a female police officer had been necessary in order to prevent the applicant from being shackled. The Regional Court found that the right provided by no. 10 of the Police Custody Regulations to be allowed to stay outside for 45 minutes per day in so far as the staffing and infrastructural situation permitted had not been breached. The applicant, an excellent climber, had previously shown that she was not ready to comply with the police’s orders. The Regional Court noted that the Braunschweig Police had received some 200 telephone calls of sympathisers of the applicant, some of whom had insulted the police. It had not been unlawful in these circumstances for the police not to permit visits by persons who had presented themselves at the police station without having lodged a request for a visit. In any event, the applicant had been visited by three persons while in detention, in addition to her two visits by her doctor, C., who had prescribed her necessary medication and had brought a couple of magazines. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the complaint against the law. The case has been adjourned until July 2014. The decision was made under file no. 2 BvR 1779/10. The court refused to give a reason as to why the complaint was rejected. The complaint was returned to the District Court for further proceedings. The Court decided that the case should be heard on August 25, 2010. The final decision was reached on August 31, 2010, in the case of the case against the laws of the Netherlands. The matter was decided on August 28, 2010 in the Court of Appeal’s hearing of the complaint. The issue of the legality of the law has now been resolved.

Bratterud, Attorney) was represented by their Agent, Mrs F. Platou Amble. The application was allotted no. 19905214 and was communicated to the Government on 7 June 2010. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice in Brussels. The first applicant submitted theoretical views on the subject-matter of the application with reference to a research report of 1965. The required tests were therefore superfluous, in his view. NIPO asked the Military Supreme Command whether the application should be kept secret on national security grounds, which the latter answered in the negative in March 1993. The first applicant on 27 November 1996 complained about the delays in the processing of his application. On the ground of the first applicant’s failure to comply with the time-limit of 5 November 1999, NIPo decided to discontinue (henlegge) its examination of his patent application under section 15(2) of the Patents Act. NIPO refused the application on the ground that the applicant had not made it probable that the subject-matter of the application had the alleged technical effect. NIPO informed the first applicant on 30 August 2001 that it had annulled its decision to discontinue the matter and gave him until 28 February 2002 to respond to its letter of 5 May 1999. The Board of Appeals took a different view and indicated a new formulation of the patent claims which might lead to a patent, but only for sea vessels. Thereafter, mostly both applicants acted as claimants in the relevant proceedings (to simplify “applicants” is used in the following). The applicants filed a new complaint to the Parliamentary Ombudsman on 13 March 2006 concerning the proceedings before NIPO. On 20 June 2007, the application was formally refused due to lack of novelty (see paragraph 35 below). On 20 August 2007 the applicants appealed to the Board of Appeals. On 29 November 2007, they were informed that the Board, after having examined the case, had found it clear that the conditions for granting a patent had not been fulfilled in so far as concerned aircrafts. The application might succeed in respect of a more limited field of sea vessels. In the alternative, the part of the application that related to air transport might be disjoined from that which related to sea transport. The applicants were given until 29 January 2008 to comment on the NIPO refusal of the patent requested. The Board of Appeals confirmed the refusal on 22 September 2008, albeit on a different reasoning. The applicants had been advised that in order to succeed, the patent requirements would have to be defined so as to exclude aviation, but had not been willing to do so. The application as presented did therefore not fulfil the conditions for grant of patent. The applications have apparently not challenged the Board of appeal’s decision before the Norwegian courts. The Government submitted that according to Espacenet (a database provided by EPO), the applicants had not claimed priority with respect to no. 19905214 in any of the above mentioned countries. The EPO patent claims from no. 19905214 are different from those in no. 19805214. The former had been based on additional features that had made the invention patentable. The latter was based on other features that were not patentable at the time of the invention. No.19805214 is based on the same technology as that was used in the first patent, from the same company, only with a different name. The second patent was granted by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office in 1988, and the third was granted in 1994. The first patent was awarded in 1992, the second in 1994, the third in 2000.

The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The applicant, Mr. Bengt Pudas, is a Swedish citizen born in 1959. He lives at Hedenäset, which is situated in the Municipality of Övertorneå and the County of Norrbotten, in the North of Sweden. He was granted a taxi traffic licence on 1 February 1980, and a licence to carry passengers and their goods on specified interurban routes (linjetrafik) on 20 May 1980. The licences were expressed in the form of a traffic licence and a carrying licence. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Corell for the Government, by Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant commenced his combined taxi and interurban traffic business on 20 May 1980. On 2 April 1981, the County Traffic Company of Norrbotten filed an application with the County Administrative Board for a licence to provide interurban transport on routes covered by Mr. Pudas’ second licence. The Company at the same time requested that this licence be revoked, as well as a licence held since 1973 by a certain Mr. Wälimaa. In support of its application, the Company submitted that two traffic services in two different regions were to be united into one regular service with a single time-table, to be provided by the bus service business. The applicant opposed the revocation of his licence. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Board of Transport (transportrådet), in which he alleged, inter alia, the following. The County Traffic Company’s application for a licence for the routes covered by his licence had been motivated not by any public interest in improving the transport service. Only very serious reasons, such as misconduct of the licence-holder, could justify revocation. When revoking his licence, the County Administrative Board had failed to take due account of his interests. The transport service on the routes concerned was not likely to be improved simply by being carried out by Mr. Wälimaa and others instead of by himself.

The applicant was indicted on charges of multiple fraud, insurance fraud, misuse of property and membership of a criminal gang. The applicant’s detention was prolonged on 24 February 2003 by the Kielce District Court and subsequently by the Cracow Court of Appeal on 22 April 2003. The courts relied on the same grounds as previously invoked by the District Court. They pointed to the complexity of the case and the existence of a fear of collusion, given the applicant's role in the criminal gang and the considerable number of witnesses acquainted with the applicant who had yet to give evidence. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 254 witnesses and to obtain over 300 other pieces of evidence. The applicant is accused of being part of a criminal group in Poland. eval_texts: The Golder case was referred to the Court by the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The application was first submitted in 1969; it was supplemented in April 1970 and registered under no. 4451/70. The Government’s application, which was made under Article 48 (art. 48) of the Convention, was lodged with the registry of the Court on 27 September 1973 within the period of three months laid down in Articles 32 para. 1 and 47. The purpose of the application is to submit the case for judgment by the Court. The five judges chosen were MM. R. Cassin, R. Rodenbourg, A. Favre, T. Vilhjálmsson and W. Ganshof van der Meersch. G. Balladore Pallieri assumed the office of President of the Chamber in accordance with Rule 21 para. 5. Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice, who had been elected a member of the Court in January 1974 in place of Sir Humphrey Waldock, took his seat in the Court as the elected judge of British nationality. The Government’s memorial was received at the registry on 6 March 1974 and that of the Commission - with observations by the applicant's counsel annexed - on 26 July. The Chamber, “considering that the case raise(d) serious questions affecting the interpretation of the Convention’, decided under Rule 48 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The public hearings took place on 11 and 12 October 1974 in the Human Rights Building at Strasbourg. Sidney Elmer Golder was convicted in 1965 of robbery with violence. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment in Parkhurst Prison on the Isle of Wight. In 1969, a serious disturbance occurred in a recreation area of the prison where Golder happened to be. On 26 October Golder, together with other prisoners suspected of having participated in the disturbance, was segregated from the main body of prisoners. Golder wrote to his Member of Parliament on 25 October and 1 November, asking whether he would be prosecuted for assaulting a prison officer causing bodily harm. At the hearings, the Government produced certain documents to the Court which were read to the jury. Golder wrote to the prison governor and to a Chief Constable about the disturbance of 24 October and the ensuing hardships it had entailed for him. The prison governor stopped these letters since Golder had failed to raise the subject-matter thereof through the authorised channels beforehand. On 20 March 1970, Golder addressed a petition to the Secretary of State for the Home Department, that is, the Home Secretary. He requested a transfer to some other prison and added: “I understand that a statement wrongly accusing me of participation in the events of 24th October last, made by Officer Laird, is lodged in my prison record’ “I would respectfully request permission to consult a solicitor with a view to taking civil action for libel in respect of this statement .... Alternatively, I would request that an independent examination of my record be allowed by Mrs. G.M. Bishop who is magistrate. I would accept her assurance that the libel against me has not materially harmed me except for the two weeks I spent in the separate cells, and so civil action would not be then necessary, providing that an apology was given to me for the libel ....“In England the matter of contacts of convicted prisoners with persons outside their place of detention is governed by the Prison Act 1952, as amended. Golder was released from prison on parole on 12 July 1972. He filed two complaints relating to the stopping of his letters and to the refusal of the Home Secretary to permit him to consult a solicitor. The first complaint was declared inadmissible, as all domestic remedies had not been exhausted. The second was accepted for consideration of the merits under Articles 6 para. 1 and 8 (art. 6-1, art. 8) of the Convention. The Government made objection to this opinion of the Commission but stated in their memorial that they no longer wished to argue the issue. Golder won the case on appeal and was released on parole in 1972. The Government says the right of access to the courts is not unlimited in the case of persons under detention. The Government also says that control over the applicant’s correspondence while he was in prison was a necessary consequence of the deprivation of his liberty. The refusal of the United Kingdom Government to allow the applicant to consult a lawyer was within the degree of restraint permitted, and therefore did not constitute a violation of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention. The Court is requested to reply to the questions: (1) Does Article 6 para. 6-1 secure to persons desiring to institute civil proceedings a right ofaccess to courts? (2) If Article. 6 ( art. 6). includes in general a right to access to courts, then the Court finds that the rights conferred by. Article 6 include in general the right to a hearing that is fair. “Can a convicted prisoner who wishes to write to his lawyer in order to institute civil proceedings rely on the protection given in Article 8 (art. 8) of the Convention to respect for correspondence?““ do the facts of the present case disclose the existence of a violation of Article 6 and of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights?” “Are there inherent limitations relating to this right, or its exercise, which apply to the facts in this case?’ “‘Is there a right of access to a lawyer that the convicted prisoner can claim for the purposes of civil proceedings?‘
